Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces are planning a major counteroffensive against Iran-backed Houthis in the coming days — an effort to push them away from areas on the Red Sea coast that control the Strait of Bab al-Mandeb, two U.S. officials say.
Why it matters: For the second time in recent weeks, the U.S. rebuffed Saudi pleas to join the operation and conduct airstrikes. But U.S. officials say that could change if the operation runs into problems.
The Bab al-Mandeb Strait is a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. Control over it gives the Houthis and their Iranian backer a powerful new point of leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy.
Driving the news: In recent weeks, the Houthis took over key areas of the southern Red Sea coast that control the strait. They also increased missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia. The Saudis retaliated with airstrikes against Houthi targets.
Behind the scenes: A U.S. official said the Saudis have been planning the operation for weeks and that plans were approved by Saudi leadership several days ago.
The operation will include ground forces loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen with Saudi air cover.
On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid Bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the U.S. official said.
A U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now."
Last week, President Trump was close to ordering a strike on the Houthis after a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), but eventually decided to hold off.
Between the lines: Trump is caught between wanting to help his friend and ally MBS, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East.
The U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen and saw it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said.
Zoom in: U.S. officials say the U.S. military is helping the Saudis with everything short of direct combat, mainly intelligence and targeting data.
One U.S. official said that in the last two weeks, the U.S. military provided the Saudis with more than 200 Houthi targets to strike. The official said the strikes significantly increased pressure on the Houthis.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia weighs possible offensive to retake Bab el-Mandeb
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia is preparing for a possible military offensive against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, with Riyadh considering a limited operation to retake territory around the s...
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia is preparing for a possible military offensive against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, with Riyadh considering a limited operation to retake territory around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait or a broader assault on several fronts, regional and Western officials told Reuters.
The operation could begin as soon as the coming weeks and would be led by Saudi-backed Yemeni forces on the ground, supported by Saudi airstrikes, according to six people familiar with the preparations.
The officials, who include Gulf and Yemeni officials and Western diplomats, spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing sensitive security matters.
The United States is providing intelligence, including targeting information, to support Saudi operations, while several regional and European countries are supplying mainly defensive military assistance. Saudi allies are not expected to take a direct combat role, the people said.
The planned offensive, which has not previously been reported, would seek to reverse recent Houthi advances along Yemen's western coast and restore access to the Bab el-Mandeb, a vital maritime chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
The Houthis seized control of the strait after advancing down the coast last month, giving the group greater leverage over one of the world's most important shipping corridors. The Bab el-Mandeb connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and is a major route for commercial traffic between Europe and Asia.
The officials said Riyadh is considering two main options. The first would be a focused assault around Bab el-Mandeb aimed at restoring control of the coastal areas. The second would involve a much larger, coordinated campaign across several parts of Yemen, including Al-Bayda, Marib, Taiz and Al-Jawf.
More than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilized depending on the scale of the operation, the officials said.
Saudi Arabia has concluded that it cannot return to peace negotiations with the Houthis while the group controls Bab el-Mandeb, according to Western diplomats and a Gulf official.
The timing remains uncertain. The six people familiar with the preparations gave estimates ranging from within a week to a launch after the U.S. midterm elections in early November.
Michael Ratney, a former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia, said he expected any operation to be relatively limited compared with the Saudi-led campaign launched in 2015.
He said Riyadh would have an interest in reversing the Houthis' territorial gains around Bab el-Mandeb without becoming trapped in another large-scale war.
"it would be a fairly limited operation to retake coastal areas and get back to normal maritime traffic," Ratney said.
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition supporting the internationally recognized government after the Houthis seized Sanaa and large parts of the country.
A truce reached in 2022 largely held until this year, when the Houthis resumed attacks involving missiles and drones against Saudi-linked shipping and oil infrastructure amid the wider regional conflict involving Iran.
The Houthis have emerged as one of Iran's most powerful regional allies, particularly as Hezbollah's military capabilities in Lebanon have been weakened over the past three years.
A new Saudi offensive would open another major front in a region already engulfed in conflict since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the subsequent U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
Washington remains Saudi Arabia's most powerful ally and is providing military advisers and intelligence to support Saudi air operations in Yemen, according to a Western diplomat.
But the extent of U.S. involvement could remain limited. Reuters has previously reported that President Donald Trump rejected requests from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for direct U.S. military support, including airstrikes.
Türkiye and Pakistan have also provided military equipment to Saudi Arabia under a broader defense relationship between Riyadh and its allies.
Pakistan sent four cargo aircraft carrying equipment including air defense systems, light artillery, drones and counter-drone systems to Aden last month, according to a Pakistani government official.
Pakistani military advisers are also in Saudi Arabia working with Saudi counterparts to support Yemeni forces, according to Pakistani, Gulf and Western officials.
Riyadh's concerns extend beyond the battlefield. Regional officials said Saudi Arabia is particularly focused on protecting its oil facilities and other critical infrastructure from Houthi missile and drone attacks and has asked allies for additional defensive systems.
Pakistan has deployed between 30,000 and 40,000 troops to Saudi Arabia to help protect its borders and assist with missile and drone interceptions, according to a Pakistani official. The troops arrived in waves beginning last year and following the latest escalation, the official said.
Pakistan has not decided to send troops into Yemen in a combat role, the official added.
The Pakistani and Turkish defense ministries did not respond to requests for comment.
France has also announced plans to send defensive systems and troops to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.
Any Saudi-backed ground offensive would depend heavily on Yemen's fragmented anti-Houthi forces, many of which were armed and trained by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates during earlier stages of the civil war.
The groups have struggled to maintain unity, raising questions about their ability to sustain a large-scale offensive against the Houthis.
"Many anti-Houthi forces are still not organised or prepared for the kind of sustained offensive required to push back a disciplined Houthi military force," said Yemen analyst Mohammed Albasha.
The anti-Houthi camp became more divided last winter after UAE-backed southern fighters attempted to seize territory in eastern Yemen and announced plans for secession. Saudi-backed forces eventually defeated them after a series of clashes.
Ali Shihabi, a Saudi political analyst close to government thinking, said the success of any offensive would ultimately depend on the performance of the Yemeni forces leading the ground campaign.
"The priority so far has been to defend the positions on the ground and stabilize the front, but certainly they will be going on the offensive," he said. "Success greatly depends on the quality of the performance of the local forces."
The prospect of a new offensive comes as fighting and cross-border attacks have intensified.
The Houthis said Friday that Saudi forces had carried out 94 strikes against areas under their control during the previous 24 hours. The group claimed Saudi Arabia had conducted 1,350 strikes since the latest fighting began.
Saudi Arabia's coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government said Friday that it intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched toward the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait.
The coalition said the missiles were intercepted without providing details on casualties or damage.
A day earlier, the coalition said it had intercepted two ballistic missiles over Khamis Mushait and Jazan, as well as four drones over Khamis Mushait.
Saudi Civil Defense said debris from an intercepted Houthi ballistic missile targeting residential areas fell in Khamis Mushait on Thursday, damaging several buildings and vehicles. No casualties were reported.
Khamis Mushait has been repeatedly targeted during the latest escalation. On Sept. 14, the Houthis claimed a large-scale attack involving dozens of ballistic missiles and drones against King Khalid Air Base in the city.
On Saturday, Saudi Civil Defense said shrapnel from another intercepted ballistic missile injured one person in Ahad Rafidah governorate in the Asir region, according to Saudi state media. The missile was fired Friday by the Iran-aligned Houthis, it said.

articles.title: Yemen’s army says targets Houthis in hundreds of strikes, killing 700 - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Yemen’s army says targets Houthis in hundreds of strikes, killing 700  Al JazeeraFighting Intensifies in Yemen, Raising Fresh Fears of All-Out War  The New York TimesYemen's armed forces say it is conducting strikes against Houthis in Sanaa  reuters.comSaudi Arabia launched more than 90 attacks in Yemen in 24 hours, Houthis claim - report  The Jerusalem PostHouthis say Saudi Arabia launched dozens of strikes on Yemen capital  The Times of Israel
articles.full_text:
The Yemeni army says it has carried out hundreds of strikes on the capital, Sanaa, and other areas held by the Iran-backed Houthis, as the battle for control of the country’s most populated regions intensifies.
Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces, said on Saturday that the military “executed 257 precision targeting operations” against Houthi sites, movements, and military capabilities.
The army used “warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles, and rocket launchers”, he added in a post on X.
Al-Nazili said initial estimates indicate the operations killed at least 700 Houthi rebels and destroyed “strategic and high-value military targets”, including 170 combat vehicles and heavy equipment.
The army spokesman did not mention any casualties among government forces.
The strikes “had a direct impact on the [Houthi] militia’s combat capability and limited its ability to continue its attacks against civilians in their homes and villages”, he said.
Saturday’s operations targeted Sanaa, Midi, Baqim, and the front lines in al-Jawf, Marib, al-Bayda, and Lahij, with the heaviest operational efforts concentrated around Taiz, al-Nazili added.
On Friday, al-Nazili said Yemen’s government forces had carried out nearly 500 military operations, killing or wounding 1,540 Houthi rebels in 24 hours.
Taiz focal point of clashes
The government-held city of Taiz has become a focal point of the renewed fighting.
Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, reporting from Taiz on Saturday, said the region is seeing continued escalation and intense fighting across several fronts around the city, with some of the fiercest fighting happening on its western outskirts.
The Houthis have used an exceptionally heavy volume of fire during the assault, she noted, adding that the sound of continuing artillery fire, particularly from the Houthi side targeting western areas, could still be heard.
Residents are appealing for evacuation as the shelling continues, Ali reported, adding that there have been civilian casualties in the fighting, including from a shell that hit a residential area in Dhubab, killing a baby who died from shrapnel injuries.
On the Samaa front, she said, the Houthis made advances on Friday in the mountainous area, and fierce clashes are continuing there between government forces and the rebels. Several field sources told Ali that large numbers of residents have left Samaa, something, she said, that had not happened on this scale in more than a decade.
Following those clashes, Yemeni government forces took control of the Samaa fort, southeast of the city of Taiz, after heavy fighting, the government-run Saba news agency reported.
A military source told Saba that the armed forces, backed by local popular resistance fighters from the Samaa district, secured the fort after “violent battles”, leaving dozens of Houthi fighters killed or wounded while others fled.
Key border crossing closed
On Saturday, the army’s media official Ammar al-Sami’i told Al Jazeera that the government had closed the al-Houban crossing in Taiz.
The crossing had previously been closed for nine years and was later reopened to civilians in 2024 for “humanitarian reasons”, Sami’i said, as the road is one of Yemen’s most important connections between territory held by the opposing sides. It connects Houthi-held al-Houban to government-held Taiz city.
Sami’i said security reasons are behind the closure, following an attempt by the Houthis to infiltrate Taiz via the road, attacks in the vicinity and a general military build-up.
A fragile truce struck between the government and the Houthis in 2022 collapsed in July this year, and fighting in Yemen has escalated significantly since then.
In mid-September, the Houthis swept across parts of western Yemen, seizing the port city of Mocha and key strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Since then, anti-Houthi forces have largely stabilised the front lines.
Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced since the fighting restarted.
Yemen has been embroiled in civil war since the Houthis seized the capital of Sanaa in 2014, forcing the internationally recognised government to retreat to Aden.

articles.title: Flydubai plane’s “jihadist” co-pilot wanted to derail UAE-Israel ties and Abraham Accords, says Israeli minister - connectedtoindia.com
articles.summary: Flydubai plane’s “jihadist” co-pilot wanted to derail UAE-Israel ties and Abraham Accords, says Israeli minister  connectedtoindia.com
articles.full_text:
Even as praise pours in from around the world for Indian-origin pilot Captain Smit Machchhar, who saved flydubai flight FZ1073, the big question on everyone’s mind is: why did the Omani co-pilot try to cause a plane crash like 9/11?
The motive, according to Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, was that the co-pilot wanted to derail diplomatic ties between Israel and the United Arab Emirates and to damage the Abraham Accords, a landmark agreement in the Middle East.
Speaking to NDTV on Thursday, the Israeli foreign minister confirmed that the co-pilot who stabbed Captain Smit Machchhar on the Dubai-Tel Aviv flydubai flight — with the intention of hijacking or crashing the plane — was an Omani national, and that Israel would push for his extradition.
Describing the nature of the incident, Sa’ar said that it was a “jihadist terror attack”. He added that though there was no evidence yet, the main motive was to damage diplomatic progress.
Sa’ar also praised Indian Captain Smit Machchhar, who was stabbed by the Omani co-pilot and bleeding inside the cockpit as the aircraft plunged because of the Omani’s sabotage. The captain managed to open the cockpit door and let people in, so that the plane and the passengers could be saved.
NDTV reported that no “official details” of the attacker had been released by either Saudi Arabia, where the crisis-hit flydubai plane made an emergency landing, or the United Arab Emirates, from where the flight took off.
The landmark Abraham Accords, first signed on 15 September 2020, “are a series of bilateral agreements brokered by the United States whose core original intent has been to normalize relations between Israel and several Arab countries”, said the Middle East Institute.
These Accords, said the institute’s summary “represented the first formal normalization of Arab-Israeli diplomatic relations since Israel’s 1994 peace treaty with Jordan and the 1979 Egypt-Israel agreement following negotiations at Camp David”.
“The name ‘Abraham Accords’ was chosen to emphasize [upon] the shared Abrahamic roots of Judaism, Islam, and Christianity — the majority faiths of the original participant countries and their diplomatic convener,” it said.
At the time, Palestinians did not react well to the Abraham Accords. Explaining the reaction of the Arab World to the Accords, a November 2020 blog post on the website of The Chicago Council on Global Affairs said: “According to a poll by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, 80 percent of Palestinians ‘describe their feelings towards [the Abraham Accords] as: treason, abandonment, and insult.’”
Then, of course, came the Hamas terrorist attack on Israel in October 2023, carried out from the Palestinian enclave of Gaza. And that date, October 7, changed everything in the Middle East all over again. The region has not known any lasting peace since then.
However, the Israeli diplomatic relationship with the United Arab Emirates has endured the Gaza war and the more recent Iran war.
Speaking about the heroic Indian pilot, Captain Smit Machchhar, and the quick thinking of Israeli passengers who overpowered the Omai saboteur in the cockpit — and saved the plan from losing altitude any further — the Israeli minister said, “We are thankful for the bravery and courage of Captain Smit Machchhar. By being able to open the door of the cockpit after he was stabbed, he saved the flight and the passengers.
“And there was the bravery of the Israeli passengers who took over the stabber, the co-pilot, and made it possible for another crew, two additional pilots who were on the plane, to take over the flight and make sure this tragedy was prevented.”
Speaking to NDTV’s Aditya Raj Kaul, minister Gideon Sa’ar said, “It is really bravery upon bravery. If you think about statistics, it’s unbelievable to get out of this difficult situation.”
Sa’ar praised the citizens of Israel and India for being united in fighting terrorism.

articles.title: Gaza war could have ended a year earlier, says ex Israeli hostage negotiator - The Times of India
articles.summary: Gaza war could have ended a year earlier, says ex Israeli hostage negotiator  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Former Israeli hostage negotiator Major General (retd) Nitzan Alon has said Israel could have ended the Gaza war about a year earlier and secured the release of all its remaining hostages without significantly compromising its other strategic objectives.
According to Al Jazeera, Alon made the remarks during a Washington Institute for Near East Policy webcast on October 2, arguing that Israel could have reached the position it ultimately achieved “much earlier, maybe a year earlier or so”. He said the prolonged war may have cost the lives of hostages who could otherwise have been brought home alive.
Alon, who served as the Israeli military's point person for hostage negotiations during the war, said Israel's insistence on achieving “total victory” over Hamas before accepting a comprehensive deal was based on a false premise.
He argued that the October 2025 ceasefire and hostage agreement demonstrated that Israel could have achieved its broader strategic objectives while reaching a deal much earlier.
Alon said the decision to continue the war also had a human cost, arguing that an earlier agreement could have brought some hostages home alive and potentially saved thousands of lives on both sides.
He said Israel “could have and should have” shortened the war and returned the hostages earlier.
The October 2025 ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas came into effect on October 10, 2025, under a US-backed plan aimed at ending the Gaza war and securing the release of the remaining Israeli hostages.
Under the first phase of the deal, Hamas agreed to release all 20 living Israeli hostages, while Israel agreed to release Palestinian prisoners and detainees and withdraw its forces to agreed positions in Gaza.
The October 2025 deal came nearly two years after the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, in which 251 people were abducted and taken to Gaza.
The attack killed more than 1,200 people, according to Israeli figures, triggering Israel’s military campaign in Gaza and a prolonged effort to secure the release of the hostages.

articles.title: UAE’s Mubadala leads as Mena SWFs spend Dh374 billion despite US-Iran war - Khaleej Times
articles.summary: UAE’s Mubadala leads as Mena SWFs spend Dh374 billion despite US-Iran war  Khaleej Times
articles.full_text:
Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala was once again the most acquisitive sovereign investor in the Middle East and North Africa (Mena) region, deploying $26.2 billion (Dh96.15 billion) in the first nine months of 2026.
According to Global SWF’s 2026 Mena Playbook, Mena sovereign investors as a group deployed $102 billion (Dh374 billion) across 245 transactions in the period to September 30, representing 39 per cent of all dealmaking by state-owned investors globally, below the levels of 2023-25 in both absolute and relative terms.
Stay up to date with the latest news. Follow KT on WhatsApp Channels.
Mubadala’s total includes capital deployed by its subsidiaries Adic, Mubadala Capital and MGX, which took part in multi-billion financing rounds for OpenAI, Anthropic and Databricks.
It is followed by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) with $14 billion, the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (Adia) with $12.2 billion, L’imad with $10.8 billion and the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA) with $10.3 billion.
Year-end projection
If the current pace continues, Mena funds will deploy $136 billion in 2026, the report says.
That would be well below 2025, when PIF’s takeover of EA boosted the total, but still the second-highest year on record. The projected 327 deals would also be the second-highest number on record, behind only 2019, driven by smaller but more frequent technology investments.
Sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) and public pension funds from the rest of the world invested $160 billion by the end of the third quarter, more than in the whole of 2025.
Most Gulf funds are on course to invest more in 2026 than their 2020-25 annual average, the report says, including Qatar’s QIA and Kuwait’s KIA, which may be tapped by their governments.
Where the money is going
The US remains the preferred destination, taking 45 per cent of the value invested by Mena funds, followed by China including Hong Kong (10 per cent), the UK (7 per cent) and Singapore (3 per cent). Almost a fifth of the $102 billion was deployed within funds' home economies, while 81 per cent went abroad. The UAE received $18.2 billion.
Technology, including artificial intelligence-related rounds, was the most popular sector, accounting for 28 per cent of deals by volume and almost 30 per cent by value. Infrastructure took 22 per cent and financial services 14 per cent. Real estate fell to just 5 per cent of volume and 11 per cent of value.
Iran war pressure
The report says the Mena region has been significantly affected by the Iran-US war and the disruption to global trade and energy supply caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Financial systems and markets continue to operate, however, and some countries have coped better than expected.
The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) remains heavily reliant on oil, with 67 per cent of GDP coming from oil exports. Kuwait reported a budget deficit of $23.1 billion by March 31 and Qatar $5.8 billion by June 30, which could mean fresh withdrawals from the KIA and the first-ever tapping of the QIA.
As a result, the industry’s assets under management could fall for the first time since 2015, with a short-term impact on liquidity and global dealmaking.
Long-term outlook
The report expects a recovery by the end of the decade. Mena SWFs, which manage $6.1 trillion today, could reach $8.8 trillion by 2030, a compound annual growth rate of 9.6 per cent. Pension funds, central banks and family offices are forecast to grow more slowly, at between 2.5 per cent and 6 per cent a year. Together, Mena state-owned investors are projected to manage $13 trillion by 2030, up from US$9.7 trillion this year.
Some GCC countries are rethinking their fiscal strategies because of the war, and new direct and indirect taxes may be introduced within the next year, the report adds.
State-owned investors still control 65 per cent of the market capitalisation of the 971 entities listed in the GCC, according to the report.
Only eight initial public offerings (IPOs) have been completed this year, and GCC market capitalisation has stayed flat at US$4 trillion.
Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) has not slowed because of the conflict and is on track to register more companies in 2026 than ever before, the report says. It adds that Abu Dhabi has slipped to second place behind Oslo in the latest World City Ranking. As of September 30, 620 financial firms were licensed to operate from the free zone.
The playbook also studies the overlap between SWFs and royal family offices through the family trees of the GCC's ruling families, and ranks all 170 Mena sovereign investors. It also lists 400 IPOs completed on regional exchanges between January 2017 and September 2026.

articles.title: Can the Abraham Accords stay on track after the flydubai attack? - All Israel News
articles.summary: Can the Abraham Accords stay on track after the flydubai attack?  All Israel News
articles.full_text:
Just days after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu returned from the United Arab Emirates, where he met with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan amid signs of renewed regional cooperation, an Omani co-pilot allegedly tried to crash a flydubai flight carrying more than 170 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
Israeli media reported that Netanyahu’s UAE visit also included an expanded meeting with representatives from Saudi Arabia, Morocco, Egypt, Kuwait, Bahrain, Libya, Oman and the United States. However, those countries have not publicly confirmed their participation. The talks reportedly focused on regional security and cooperation, raising hopes that Israel’s relationships with its Arab neighbors could finally begin moving forward again after nearly three years of war.
Then came the attempted attack.
The Omani co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain and attempted to crash the aircraft before passengers intervened. Additional pilots aboard the flight took control, safely landing the plane in Saudi Arabia. Israeli officials have described the incident as a possible terrorist attack, although investigators are still working to determine the attacker’s precise motive and whether he acted alone.
In the immediate aftermath, flights between Israel and the UAE were disrupted, leaving Israeli travelers stranded and prompting Israeli carriers to organize repatriation flights.
The incident came at an especially sensitive moment for Israel’s relations with the Arab world. Direct flights between Israel and Marrakech are resuming, with Israeli airlines expanding service this fall – another sign that ties with Morocco are beginning to recover as the region moves beyond the October 7 war.
Those close to the diplomatic process do not believe the attempted attack will derail the warming relationships. But they say it serves as a stark reminder of how fragile those ties remain and how much work Israel still has to do if it wants to restore the Abraham Accords to where they stood on October 6, 2023, let alone expand them further.
Noam Meirov, a Middle East expert specializing in regional business relations and partnerships, particularly among the Abraham Accords countries, told ALL ISRAEL NEWS that he sees the accords today as somewhere between surviving and thriving.
“I am not going to say that everything is all right [with the Accords],” he said. “But I am not pessimistic and don’t think they were destroyed. I’m somewhere in the middle.”
He said the war in Gaza and across the region “strategically challenged” the accords. Yet the fact that the relationships are beginning to pick up again in any capacity, he said, demonstrates both their resilience and the “mutual ground” on which Israel and its Abraham Accords partners continue to stand.
The Abraham Accords currently include normalization agreements between Israel and the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Morocco. Sudan also agreed to normalize relations with Israel, although the process has stalled due to the country's ongoing instability. Kazakhstan also officially joined the accords in November 2025.
“We have similar needs and values,” Meirov said, noting that, from his perspective, all parties are “truly against radicalism of all sorts” in the region, especially “Iran as the major exporter of radicalism in the region.”
He said the countries also share common business and innovation interests, including a focus on new technologies and regional economic growth, much of which began developing to varying degrees after the accords were signed.
But Meirov acknowledged that the relationships built through the Abraham Accords have been battered over the past three years, as the war against Hamas in Gaza strained Israel’s standing across the Arab world. He said negative coverage of Israel throughout the region, particularly from outlets such as Qatar’s Al Jazeera, has contributed to that deterioration.
The challenge now, he said, is for both Israel and its Arab partners to make a deliberate decision to rebuild what has been lost.
“That means both sides need to continue to actively invest in the accords from a business perspective, and a public diplomacy perspective, and from a political perspective to strive to expand the accords,” Meirov said.
He stressed that regaining the momentum that existed before October 7 will not happen automatically.
“Before the war we were in amazing momentum, on the verge of signing this normalization agreement with Saudi Arabia,” Meirov noted. “Now we're further away from that than October 6. To get there, we need to recreate momentum with other countries and with the countries who have already signed the accords.”
Part of that process, he said, will require Israel and the Arab countries to clearly articulate their vision for the region, including that they “see Israel as an integral part of the Middle East, and to teach that to their children.”
Fatema Alharbi, Gulf Affairs director for the NGO Sharaka, expressed similar sentiments. Speaking to ALL ISRAEL NEWS from Bahrain, she said that “we are living in very, very challenging times, and you cannot predict what will happen next.”
Alharbi said she hopes the Israeli elections will result in “a more moderate coalition” that could help advance and expand the accords.
Despite the uncertainty, Meirov said he remains hopeful that the next phase will include countries that have so far remained outside the Abraham Accords.
“I do hope that we will see new countries joining the accords soon,” Meirov said. “There were countries rumored to have really gone through a dramatic change, an understanding that Israel is a positive part of this region throughout the last three years, and I'm praying that hopefully they'll go public about it and normalize relationships with Israel as soon as possible.”

articles.title: Can anyone stop the Houthis? Yemen’s civil war is set to go global - unherd.com
articles.summary: Can anyone stop the Houthis? Yemen’s civil war is set to go global  unherd.com
articles.full_text:
Yemen has always been defined by its topography. A landscape of narrow coastal plains, mountainous highlands, and a desert interior, has helped preserve tribal identities, blurring and softening sharp religious divisions. If a very modern, post-1979 battle between Sunnis and Shi’ites now defines the country’s politics, a rugged and inescapable geography continues to impose itself. This is clear enough with the Zaydi Shi’ites, now better known by the name of a martyred Islamist leader: Hussein al-Houthi. Combining a deep knowledge of their country’s landscape with revolutionary zeal, the Houthis have coalesced into an unrivaled fighting force, as well as Iran’s best allies in its war against America and Israel – costing Tehran surprisingly little money.
Indeed, the more you learn about the Houthis, the less surprising it becomes that the group should have embarrassed the US Navy in 2024 and 2025 (in a foretaste of the second Iran war, Washington simply gave up firing its expensive missiles at Houthi forces), and fought a large Sunni-Arab coalition to a standstill between 2015 and 2019. Despite intense bombardments, and serious battlefield defeats, the Houthis have retained Sana’a, Yemen’s capital which they conquered in 2014. Only the Israelis, who briefly got into a missile exchange with the Houthis in 2025, have managed to deter them: they went after the Houthis’ oil supplies, energy infrastructure, ports, airports, and, perhaps most important, senior personnel. Sure enough, the Houthis stopped firing at Israel. But either way, it’s little wonder that the Houthis are now back, seizing land along the Red Sea littoral and the islands of Perim and Greater and Lesser Hanish, thereby putting into jeopardy Saudi Arabia’s capacity to export oil via its east-west pipeline.
Without outside support, Sunni Yemenis would have had no chance on the battlefield against their Shi’ite countrymen. The Houthis have received some support from Hezbollah and Iran — but not nearly on the level that Sunnis have received from foreigners since the Sixties. Islamic history has occasionally seen fervent, martial highland peoples descend into conflict with more numerous lowland believers — and usually get the better of them. The Houthis are in this line: mountain Shi’ites who have managed to gain the upper hand over the cosmopolitan and fractious Sunnis.
During the North Yemen Civil War (1962–1970), the Zaydi royalists of the old Imamate survived a massive assault by the republican forces that had overthrown them. The Republicans included predominantly Sunni Yemenis, but also Zaydi Arab nationalists, and were backed by around 70,000 Egyptian troops equipped with Soviet tanks and aircraft. The Zaydi royalists, meanwhile, adopted highly effective guerrilla tactics. Again and again, they descended from their mountain strongholds, absorbing heavy losses. They were not able to capture Sana’a — but they were repeatedly able to regroup and return to the fight.
The war today is vastly more sectarian. Few Zaydis now fight alongside Sunnis, giving the more cohesive, dogged, and fit Houthi forces the advantage.
Still, since the Nineties, support from Shi’ites in the wider region has been crucial in shaping Houthi objectives. The Islamic Republic of Iran and Lebanon’s Hezbollah have actively sought to convert Zaydis, who follow a different creed and jurisprudence. These efforts have met some success: perhaps as many as 10% of Zaydis have accepted Iran’s “Twelver” branch of Shi’ism. These conversions are, however, just icing on the cake. Before the Lebanese and Iranians came calling, Zaydism as a faith had considerable revolutionary potential. Historically, Yemen’s Shi’ites have had activist imams: religious leaders who could also command troops. Where the Twelver Shi’ites of Iran, Iraq, and Lebanon could — before the Iranian Revolution in 1979 — sometimes look askance at clerics assuming political power, the Zaydis had no such reservations. Zaydi imams ruled as kings, more or less continuously, from 897 to 1962, when nationalist forces toppled the imamate. The main interruptions came during two periods of Ottoman rule, from 1538 to 1635 and from 1872 to 1918. Even then, the imams did not simply disappear: they retreated into the mountains, where they continued to exercise religious authority and, at times, lead armed resistance to the Ottomans.
Today, a spiritual alignment has unquestionably taken place — and a significant slice of the Zaydi community is now inside the Iranian orbit. The Houthis’ anthem — “God is the Greatest, Death to America, Death to Israel, Curse be upon the Jews, Victory to Islam” — would have seemed bizarre to most Zaydis before the radical revivalist movement of al-Houthi. Cursing distant America, or Jews as if they were a global menace, or even Israel as a part of a defining, individual creed would have been too modern.
More or less at war with the “official”, internationally-recognized government of Yemen since 2004, the country’s Shi’ites are on a winning streak. Indeed, since the Saudis, Emiratis, and a coalition of other Arab states tried to humble them from 2015 to 2018, the Houthis’ regional ambitions have grown. They have created their own supply and sanctions-resistant support networks in the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, sometimes piggybacking on the Iranians, sometimes moving independently. With Iranian assistance, they figured out how to defy a Saudi naval blockade and US satellite reconnaissance. Indeed, the Houthis have been able to incorporate Iranian strategic planning into their own ambitions as well as any Iranian proxy. They have proven sharp adopters of Iranian-supplied drones and missiles, learning quickly how to build projectiles from either clandestinely delivered parts or from scratch — indeed, they have proved enthusiastic adopters of AI.
It’s also a foregone conclusion that if Iran can gain control of the Strait of Hormuz and charge tolls, the Houthis will attempt to do the same through dominating the Bab al-Mandab, the chokepoint for all trade moving through the Suez Canal — as well as for Saudi oil via its pipeline. Even if Iran fails to dominate the Persian Gulf, indeed, the odds are that the Houthis will still try to curtail Saudi shipping. If successful, the Houthi’s ambitions – and greed — may direct them towards other commercial shipping.
Yemen is a very poor country, and the Zaydi mountain heartland now offers little of the trade that once made the Zaydi elite relatively rich within it. Enormous anger towards Saudis is common. When I was traveling among Yemeni Shi’ites before 9/11 and I needed a conversation starter, aspersing Saudis always worked. So targeting Saudi shipping is a given for the Houthis; and preying on others could become an irresistible financial temptation if they control the Bab al-Mandab. Raiding British and Indian trade in the Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean in the 18th century was very good business for pirates of the Arabian Peninsula until the Royal Navy and Marines convinced them otherwise.
The US maintains Camp Lemonnier, its only permanent military base in Africa and the operational hub of US Africa Command, just across the Bab al-Mandab in Djibouti. President Trump wasn’t persuaded of the merits of using it to deny the Houthis a partial victory against his Navy in 2025. It’s a good bet that Trump will default the responsibility for stopping Houthi extortion onto European navies, especially the French, who also have a naval base at Djibouti. Trump is perennially capricious — but also firm in his conviction that Europeans are freeloaders.
Nonetheless, the problem that the West has with the Houthis is also a microcosm of the problem that the United States has with Iran: there is no clever, low-cost way to neutralize the enemy’s power. When, in 2015, he was the Saudi defense minister, Crown Prince Muhammad bin Salman clearly understood the long-term threat that the Houthis posed to his kingdom. The prince’s execution of the subsequent war may have been abysmal, but his analysis wasn’t. Neither the Saudis, nor the Emiratis, nor the Egyptians, nor the Jordanians, nor the Americans, nor the Europeans have been willing to put a lot of boots on the ground long enough to neutralise the Houthi war machine. Cairo’s unpleasant experience in Yemen in the Sixties — “Egypt’s Vietnam” — remains in the DNA of Middle Eastern military men. The combined Arab assault on the Houthis from 2015 onwards revealed a wariness of replicating the approach the Egyptians had used — trying to take the Houthis on in their heartland.
The Houthis know this. So do the Iranians, who have seen the most independent of their proxies become their most consequential ally. The strategic potential of Yemen’s Shi’ites now dwarfs the contribution of the Levantine Hezbollah to Iran’s remarkably consistent goal of weakening the West and their allied Arab governments in the Middle East. The Houthis aren’t nearly as sophisticated as the Levantine Shi’ites, who rival the Iranians in their formative contribution to the development of radical Shi’ism, and have proved rather better than the Iranians in maintaining the crucial interpersonal relations between Arab militants.
Yet the Houthis, who not long ago were mostly farmers and shepherds, have thrived in a primitive environment. Their relations with Somalia’s Al-Shabaab — a Salafist jihadist outfit, which in 2012 pledged allegiance to Al-Qaeda and has often shown a savagery that rivals Islamic State’s — clearly show the Houthis have, like the Iranians, an ecumenical disposition toward anti-Shi’ite but anti-Western Sunni Muslim radicals. If left alone, the Houthis might well develop further, becoming emissaries of Iranian mischief far beyond the Gulf of Aden. Some Islamic militants — the Taliban in Afghanistan; Hamas in Gaza — keep their violence local. They don’t become members of the “global jihad” even though they may host or associate with Muslim radicals who do. B

articles.title: The Red Sea, Its Strategic Complication, The Multiple Actors And Ethiopia’s Quest For Access To The Sea - Borkena
articles.summary: The Red Sea, Its Strategic Complication, The Multiple Actors And Ethiopia’s Quest For Access To The Sea  Borkena
articles.full_text:
The Red Sea area is becoming contentious. Ethiopia is pushing for access to the Sea. Egypt is trying to be a major actor. Saudi, Turkey, Eritrea, Djibouti, Sudan and Somaliland have vested interests. Somalia is serving Turkey’s and Egypt’s interest as a backup to the southern flank to the red sea from the Indian Ocean. Major Global powers are also interested. Therefore a comprehensive strategy analysis about this interrelated and complex interest in the red sea area is critical.
The Red Sea is no longer simply a maritime-security issue. It is becoming a single strategic system linking the Horn of Africa, Nile Basin, Arabian Peninsula, Gulf, Suez Canal and Indian Ocean. Ethiopia’s search for reliable sea access is one of the forces changing the system created after Eritrean secession from Ethiopia. The Red Sea issue is now interacting with much larger contests involving Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, UAE, Israel, Iran, the US, China, Russia and European powers.
The most important point is that the central context is not simply “who controls the Red Sea”. It is who can acquire enough strategic leverage over the ports, islands, military facilities, shipping lines and political states around the Red Sea to prevent rivals from becoming dominant.
The situation has become considerably more urgent in 2026 because instability around the Bab el-Mandeb is again demonstrating how quickly regional conflicts can become a global economic problem. Recent Houthi advances towards the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb strait have heightened the strategic importance of Djibouti, Eritrea, Sudan, and the Somali Coast as well as the giant land mass in the neighbourhood- Ethiopia.
A. The emerging Red Sea strategic system: the competition in this strategic area could be divided into five overlapping layers
The first layer is a maritime layer where the central quest is who can influence Bab el- Mandeb, ports, island, and shipping. The second layer is the military where the central quest is who can establish bases, naval facilities, airfields and surveillance networks. The third layer is economic where the central quest is who controls ports, logistics, trade corridors and investments. The fourth layer is political where the Central quest is which government became aligned with which external powers. The fifth layer is strategic and geography where the central quest is can Ethiopia, Egypt Turkey, Sudan, Saudi Arabia, Iran or others prevent rivals from dominating the region. Here the key factor is the active attempt to block Ethiopia from having access to the Red Sea coordinated by Egypt with the support of Eritrea, Sudan, and tactical but hidden tacit understanding with Saudi, Somalia and Djibouti.
These layers of strategic activities overlap. For example, Berbera is simultaneously a commercial port, an Ethiopian sea access option, Somaliland sovereignty issue, a Somali territorial integrity issue, a UAE/DP world economic interest, an Israeli strategic interest and a potential military position near Bab el-Mandeb. This is why apparently separate disputes are becoming interconnected.
B. Ethiopia is a principal actor that wants it’s rightful historical access to the Red Sea that was illegally taken away be reinstated
Ethiopia’s position is fundamentally different from most other regional actors. Ethiopia is (a) the country with the largest population and land mass in the Horn. (b) It is one of Africa’s largest militaries. (c) Geographically adjacent to the Red Sea. Its Sovereign Coastline was unfairly and illegally taken away during Eritrea secession with an illegal agreement between EPL and TPLF. (d) Ethiopia is economically dependent on Maritime trade (e) and heavily dependent on Djibouti literally keeping Ethiopia hostage with the continuous price increase and services that demanded heavy improvement. (f) Ethiopia is strategically dissatisfied with permanent land locked status created by short sited tribal warriors who did not properly understand the Strategic, Economic and Political stranglehold of the historical right and interest of hundreds of millions of people. Consequently Ethiopia increasingly views access to the Sea as a Strategic rather than merely commercial requirement.
The Ethiopian position has several components. Economically, it wants alternative ports, lower logistic costs; reduce dependency on Djibouti, diversified import export corridors, greater bargaining power over port fees and transit, and long-term maritime structure.
Strategically Ethiopia also wants to avoid becoming strategically dependent upon another state’s good will. That is particularly important because 130+ million people and one of Africa’s largest economies is effectively dependent on external territory for maritime access.
The Ethiopian military needs a permanent naval facility, military base or sovereign controlled maritime position where its strategy and security depends. The surrounding military balance, the multiple numbers of countries with strategic interest and involvement requires Ethiopia to do so. Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia are actually opposing Ethiopia’s access to the sea. To keep Ethiopia landlocked and encircled. A military and strategic situation which Ethiopia needs to break out since the intention is hostile and confinement.
As a result Ethiopia signalled through the 2024 Somaliland initiative that it would one way or another fulfill its military, strategic, and economic needs. The 2024 Somaliland initiative potentially indicated Ethiopia can have a strategic presence on the Gulf of Eden and Red Sea area one way or the other with cooperation or non-cooperation. The subsequent Turkish mediated Ethiopia Somalia re-approchement reduced the immediate tension but did not eliminate Ethiopia’s underlying strategic requirement.
C. For Egypt the Red Sea is an extension of the Nile question: Egypt’s strategic calculation is much broader than simply protecting the Suez Canal. Cairo has three major calculations
1. Egypt regards Ethiopia’s growing power as a potential long term strategic challenge because of the Nile and GERD dispute where 86% of the Nile water flow comes from Ethiopia.
2. Red Sea security: Egypt wants to remain one of the principal Arab African powers influencing Sudan, Eritrea, Somalia, Djibouti and red sea military security.
3. Preventing an Ethiopian military presence in the red sea: this is probably the most critical and sensitive issue. Egyptians are trying to limit Ethiopians military and naval presence in the Red Sea as a bargaining power over the Nile.
Egypt’s geographic and geopolitical, as well as military strategy has several possible pressure points around Ethiopia. From the north through Sudan; from the east through Eritrea; from the southeast from Somalia, and then maritime pressure through the red sea. In addition it puts its political pressure through the Arab League and African diplomat networks as well as using its proximity to the US. Through this Egypt is generally working to create a strategy containment and encirclement of Ethiopia.
The recent important development is Egypt’s increasing relationship with Eritrea. Cairo and Asmara held a high-level Summit in June 2026, reinforcing the strategic importance of the Eritrean coast in Egyptian calculation.
Egypt therefore has an incentive to maintain relationships with countries surrounding Ethiopia without necessarily seeking direct confrontation.
D. Eritrea:
Geography has given Eritrea strategic value. It is extraordinarily important because it possessed something Ethiopia desperately wanted and exploited it to the maximum. That is the Sovereign red sea Coastline that Ethiopia desperately needs based on historic rights and political injustice that deliberately denied her one of his foremost ports.
Eritrea currently has Masawa, Assab, long red sea coastline, proximity to Ethiopia, proximity to Bab el- Mandeb, proximity to Yemen and the Strategic depth between the Gulf and the Horn.

People ride their motorbikes under a billboard showing Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi with a phrase in Arabic that reads, "master of words and deeds," in Sanaa, Yemen, Sept. 21, 2026. | Osamah Abdulrahman/AP
Nahal Toosi is POLITICO’s senior foreign affairs correspondent. She has reported on war, genocide and political chaos in a career that has taken her around the world. Her reported column delves into the decision-making of the global national security and foreign policy establishment — and the fallout that comes from it.
President Donald Trump has done a lot this year to live up to the criticism that he is reckless. But in a faceoff with a heavily armed, religiously driven regime that’s threatening a critical waterway, he’s acting remarkably restrained.
Trump may have no choice: It’s really hard to deal with the Houthis.
As the Yemeni militant group pursues a new offensive against U.S. ally Saudi Arabia, Trump has — for now — resisted entering the fray with American airstrikes. He has made clear he isn’t inclined to abandon a ceasefire the U.S. reached with the Houthis after weeks of clashes last year, despite Saudi requests for more help as the Houthis threaten oil and other commerce in the Red Sea.
Trump has stressed that the Houthis are promising not to fire on U.S. ships.
“The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” Trump said last month.
This is a notably cautious position from a man who has shown a big appetite for political risk this year, whether it’s by launching a war on Iran, abducting Venezuela’s president or imposing an energy blockade in an effort to oust the Cuban regime.
Standard disclaimer here: Trump frequently changes his mind, often for surprising reasons. He could end up striking the Houthis while you read this column.
Still, Trump’s unwillingness so far to break the ceasefire with the Houthis is a potential sign that he has learned some hard lessons about the battlefront, including when to avoid it.
The Houthis wouldn’t mind this being the case. In texts to me, a Houthi official sidestepped questions about the group’s views on Trump but stressed that the ceasefire with the U.S. stands.
“We do not believe there is any reason for the United States to get involved in Yemen again,” the official wrote. I granted the official, and others, anonymity to discuss sensitive issues.
Besides, Trump has other headaches. That includes deciding whether and when to resume bombing the regime in Tehran.
“The war with Iran is unresolved, so I can understand why he’s not keen to open up another front,” Tim Lenderking, a former U.S. special envoy to Yemen who has negotiated with the Houthis, told me.
There are, of course, links between the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi fight. Iran’s regime supports and arms the Houthis, who control much of Yemen.
Tehran’s leaders and the Houthi hierarchy also share a striking number of characteristics, including leaders who stay in hiding and, some argue, expansionist ideals. Both the Houthis and Iran’s regime follow Shia Islam, though different strands. They both despise the U.S. and Israel. The Houthi official motto is: “God is the greatest, Death to America, Death to Israel, A curse upon the Jews, Victory to Islam.” Amid outside pressure, they each seek to control maritime passages key to global trade: Iran in the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthis in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
In many ways, however, the battles are distinct.
The Houthis are more a partner than a proxy for Tehran, current and former U.S. and foreign officials familiar with the group are keen to stress. The Houthis have their own grievances, history and agenda. That agenda includes ending what the Houthis describe as a blockade on Yemen imposed by Saudi Arabia, which backs the official, but weak, Yemeni government.
“We are merely defending ourselves and our country,” the Houthi official told me.
The U.S. continues to support Saudi Arabia through efforts like intelligence-sharing and weapons sales. Washington and Riyadh have a defense agreement, and, in a boilerplate statement, the White House stressed that “if it comes down to it, the United States will always stand with Saudi Arabia and support them.”
But there’s no sign that top Trump aides are urging him to again unleash the U.S. military in the Yemen fight. Last year’s U.S. air campaign against the Houthis, Operation Rough Rider, had limited impact even though Trump claimed the Houthis “capitulated.” U.S. munition shortages, caused in part by the Iran war, have to be considered now.
I’m told that Secretary of State Marco Rubio is particularly attuned to analysts’ warnings about the dangers of jumping back into the Houthi fight.
“Rubio understands the complexity. He has a good grasp of who the players are,” said a U.S. official familiar with the administration’s Middle East policy.
Some U.S. lawmakers and former U.S. officials say it’s worth helping the Saudis by carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis, at least to degrade the Yemeni militia’s capacity. Others familiar with the region warn that even sending in U.S. ground troops may not be enough to stop the group.
The Houthis have evolved into a fearsome military force in recent years. They are manufacturing more of their own weapons, while upgrading arms sent from Iran. They are even reportedly integrating artificial intelligence into their arsenal.
“They’re amazing with these advanced conventional weapons. They would take missiles and figure out how to lighten them so that they would go farther. They did trial and error with guidance systems,” said a Western official who has closely monitored the Yemen conflict. “If nothing further came from Iran, that would hurt the Houthis, but they’d overcome it.”
April Alley, a former U.N. official who has met with the Houthis, said their ambitions are likely to grow in the years ahead.
“A lot of their leadership is really young, and they’ve kind of come up in various wars. They’ve seen themselves throughout this come out of really tight spots and kind of on top, so they’re pushing on open doors,” Alley said.
Former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden also struggled to counter the Houthis without tipping into large-scale conflict. So yes, Trump might have something in common with his Democratic predecessors.
Obama authorized at least one strike, casting it as a response to Houthi attacks aimed at U.S. ships, and his administration supported the Saudis in other ways. Biden authorized a series of strikes as the Houthis stepped up attacks at the height of the Gaza war while claiming to be acting against Israeli interests in the region. But Biden also scaled back U.S. military support for the Saudi war effort and pushed Riyadh to reach a 2022 truce with the Houthis.
Hussain Al-Bukhaiti, a pro-Houthi Yemeni journalist, argued that Saudi Arabia undermined that 2022 truce, especially by refusing to lift the blockade. The Houthis also allege the Saudis in July bombed an airport in Sanaa as an Iranian plane was about to land. The Houthis started striking back, and the truce collapsed.
Al-Bukhaiti blamed the Saudis for the suffering and displacement of numerous Yemeni civilians.
“It’s about Yemeni lives,” Al-Bukhaiti said. “What is silly is that we see that all the international community and the Saudis are crying out loud that the price of oil will increase and the price of shipping is increasing. I mean, what about Yemenis?”
I must interject here: The Houthis are highly repressive rulers and not great at governing. “Horrifying” is how one humanitarian official described life under the Houthis.
When I noted to Al-Bukhaiti that the Houthis struck the Saudis just as the kingdom is struggling to absorb the economic shock of the Iran war, he didn’t disagree that it was a tad opportunistic.
“It is not wrong when you take advantage of the weakness of your enemy, and our enemy is Saudi,” he said.
The Saudi Arabian Embassy in Washington declined to comment. Riyadh, which militarily intervened against the Houthis in 2015, views the militia and its ties to Iran as a next-door security risk that could eventually threaten Saudi territorial integrity.
Reuters reported Friday that the Saudis are planning a new assault on the Houthis in the coming weeks.
Trump likely wants to stay out of the Saudi-Houthi fight for as long as possible. It could get harder, though, if the Houthis grow more emboldened, threatening not just the Bab el-Mandeb Strait but also other parts of the region.
If Trump wants to avoid opening another front, it’s strange that he has devoted little diplomatic muscle to resolving the conflict.
Trump has not filled the role of the U.S. special envoy focused on the Saudi-Houthi fight; Lenderking, who last held that role, helped broker the 2022 truce. There is no one serving as U.S. ambassador to Yemen or Saudi Arabia. Trump’s favored negotiators, like Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, have their hands full with the conflicts in Iran, Gaza and Ukraine. It doesn’t help that the Omanis, who often act as mediators, don’t have the best relationship with the U.S. at the moment.
The Houthis have a diplomatic wing that deals with foreigners, often in Oman. Former international officials who have engaged with Houthi negotiators say they can be funny, charming and transactional, at least on a short-term basis.
That’s not to say diplomacy with the Houthis would be easy.
The main Houthi leadership is in Yemen, and the movement’s structure is hierarchical, religiously zealous and almost paranoid about the outside world.
Martin Griffiths, a former U.N. special envoy for Yemen, is the rare foreigner who has dealt directly with the top Houthi boss, Abdul-Malik Al-Houthi, in Yemen.
But those encounters were through screens in safe houses. (He thought he heard al-Houthi cough in a nearby room once.)
Ultimately, even if U.S. or other negotiators have good relations on the surface with Houthi representatives, the Houthis still keep a distance that makes it challengi

articles.title: Jared Kushner’s company has large stake in firm with Israeli military links - CNN
articles.summary: Jared Kushner’s company has large stake in firm with Israeli military links  CNN
articles.full_text:
At the same time Jared Kushner has acted as a key negotiator in the war in Gaza, his private equity company, Affinity Partners, has held the largest stake in an Israeli firm backing businesses involved in Israel’s military campaigns, a CNN investigation has found.
Kushner has skirted deeper scrutiny of this potential conflict of interest by acting as a volunteer envoy, rather than accepting a government job that would require him to disclose his finances.
In the process, Kushner has carved out an unprecedented dual role under the Trump administration – one that blends lucrative business and high-stakes politics amid a devastating war.
CNN used Israeli financial transparency laws to trace some of the military-linked investments of Phoenix Financial, a Tel Aviv-based firm that Kushner’s investment group doubled its stake in last year, shortly before Donald Trump returned to the Oval Office. Kushner later described Phoenix as Affinity’s “best investment.”
Those records, which include only a fraction of Phoenix’s holdings, show Phoenix has invested hundreds of millions of dollars into Israel’s largest arms manufacturer, Elbit Systems. Phoenix also holds stakes in at least eight other companies providing equipment for the Israeli military ranging from drones to warships to demolition machinery, CNN found.
All nine companies identified by CNN saw their stock value climb last year, with many stating the war in Gaza had driven demand for their businesses.
Affinity doesn’t directly hold a stake in the nine companies CNN identified – but it does stand to reap rewards when Phoenix makes a profit.
Since spring 2025, Kushner has been a leading administration voice in the Middle East, advising Trump and flying across the globe to negotiate with leaders including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – and even unveiling plans for rebuilding and transforming the Gaza Strip into a global tourist hub.
Kushner was a key architect of the Gaza ceasefire brokered between Israel and Hamas last October; despite that deal, Israel continues striking the enclave on a near daily basis.
CNN found no indication that Kushner’s actions as a diplomat directly affected the investments reviewed. However, his firm has reaped strong gains from its Phoenix investment, cashing out a quarter of its stake in July for more than $340 million – a return of more than five times its initial stock purchase. Owned solely by Kushner, Affinity remains Phoenix’s largest shareholder with a 7.4% stake worth more than $1 billion as of July.
Kushner has spoken candidly about both his Phoenix investment and his role as a peace broker, arguing that financial profit is the best path toward lasting peace.
“When you get an Arab and Israeli together and they start talking about a business opportunity, they forget about everything else and then they realize that there’s a lot of similarities,” Kushner told the “No Priors” podcast in September last year.
“My investors from the Middle East are now looking at Israel, and they’re saying, ‘Wait a minute, maybe there’s a benefit to having these wars done,’” he added.
But critics say Kushner’s financial entanglements combined with his unofficial role as a powerful White House representative to a war-torn region raise questions about whether he’s acting in the best interests of taxpayers or his own bottom line.
“There are always people who profit from war or government policies. The difference is that the people profiting should not be the people making the decisions to make that policy. And that is what is happening here,” said Cynthia Brown, chief ethics counsel for Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington.
An attorney for Kushner told CNN Kushner has “never participated in or directed Phoenix’s decisions” on where to invest, adding he had “no involvement in the decision to purchase, hold or sell any of the nine companies” highlighted by CNN and has never been on Phoenix’s board. They added, “any suggestion that Jared’s diplomatic work influenced Phoenix’s investments in the companies you identify, or vice versa, is incorrect.”
Kushner, however, told Forbes last September that he maintains “a very active dialogue” with the financial group, meeting every few weeks with its leadership.
His attorney confirmed to CNN this statement was accurate at the time and that Kushner “regularly spoke with Phoenix management about the company, broader market trends and potential strategic opportunities.”
But they added that Kushner’s interaction with Phoenix’s management had significantly reduced since becoming “substantially more engaged in volunteer public-service and diplomatic efforts.”
Some of Phoenix’s stakes in companies tied to the Israeli military came before Kushner’s firm became the largest shareholder. Others, including a company making electronic fuzes for shells used in Gaza, and another that manufactures parts for Israeli tanks, came after.
Phoenix declined to address what appeared to be inconsistencies in the labeling of some of its public reports. Two forensic accountants in Israel separately reviewed the records and concluded, despite those inconsistencies, the filings analyzed by CNN are Phoenix’s holdings. These include investments CNN identified that were made by Phoenix in the military-linked firms.
The documents show details for only one part of Phoenix’s portfolio, and do not include assets in retirement accounts or stakes held in companies through mutual funds, corporate bonds and other securities, the accountants confirmed.
Though Phoenix did not provide comment on CNN’s findings, a company spokesperson noted that the firm is “regulated” and that “shareholder value is derived primarily from operating performance rather than investment returns.”
As a private company, Affinity, like Kushner, is not required under US law to disclose where it invests. Kushner revealed in March that Affinity had made 28 investments so far, but the size of its stake in Phoenix relative to the rest of its holdings remains unclear.
A spokesperson for the White House dismissed concerns over a potential conflict of interest between Kushner’s roles as volunteer and businessman, calling them a “tired narrative that Democrats have pushed against President Trump, his family, and his administration for a decade.”
“Jared Kushner’s personal business activities have nothing to do with his diplomatic engagements, which he conducts on a volunteer basis at the President’s request,” said White House principal deputy press secretary Anna Kelly. She cited his “record of success” in past diplomatic efforts, including helping broker the Abraham Accords, the normalization agreements between Israel and several Arab states during Trump’s first term.
Democrats, though, have sought to open new investigations into Kushner’s activities in the region, probes that could heat up if they retake control of the House in the midterms. In a letter sent to Kushner in April promising an investigation by the House Judiciary Committee, Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin described Kushner’s dual roles as a “completely irreconcilable and unethical” decision that he said “has been haunting American foreign policy since President Trump returned to Washington in 2025.”
‘The president asked me to get more involved’
Kushner incorporated the company he later transformed into the Miami-based Affinity Partners on January 21, 2021, just a day after Trump’s first term ended. Six months later, the firm secured a $2 billion investment from the Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) – Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund led by the Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, with whom he had built a close relationship during Trump’s first term in office. At the time, the fund’s board overruled a group of PIF advisers who cautioned against the investment, warning in part of “the inexperience of the Affinity Fund management,” the New York Times reported.
Cash injections from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates followed, as did a string of investments that included stakes in the Abu Dhabi-backed Zamp, which operates fast food restaurants across Brazil, and the Germany-based smart fitness company EGYM.
In 2023, Affinity agreed to make its first investment in Israel, buying a 15% stake in the Shlomo Group’s car rental and credit business for $150 million.
The next year, Affinity bought a 4.95% stake in Phoenix Financial for $128.5 million. Phoenix is one of Israel’s largest financial groups, offering services spanning insurance, pensions and asset management. Affinity then roughly doubled its stake in Phoenix five days before Trump was sworn back into office, becoming Phoenix’s largest shareholder.
Kushner has described the investment as a bet on Israel’s economic strength.
“Investing in Phoenix in July 2024 was a decision rooted in my belief in Israel’s resiliency and the fundamentals of Phoenix’s business,” Kushner told Bloomberg after receiving the nod from authorities to double his stake.
Affinity’s renewed bet on Phoenix came amid Israel’s escalating war in Gaza, which began in retaliation for Hamas’ deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, in which more than 1,200 Israelis were killed. Israel’s campaign, which officials have argued is necessary for national security, has killed more than 74,000 people, according to Palestinian health ministry figures, and been described as disproportionate by critics. An independent United Nations inquiry found Israel’s military actions in Gaza amounted to genocide, a characterization Israel has repeatedly rejected.
Kushner soon stepped into a central role in mediating the conflict. But unlike during Trump’s first term, when Kushner was a senior adviser in the White House and helped craft key deals like the Abraham Accords, this time he avoided taking on a formal role.
Instead, Kushner began acting as an unofficial adviser to his father-in-law starting in May 2025, as the war reached a fever pitch.

Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Open Top Container market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global open top container market represents a specialized yet vital segment of the intermodal freight industry, catering to the transport of over-height, heavy, and bulk cargo that cannot be accommodated by standard dry containers. As of 2026, the market is navigating a complex landscape shaped by post-pandemic supply chain realignments, shifting trade patterns, and accelerating infrastructure development across emerging economies. The forecast period to 2035 indicates a trajectory closely tied to project cargo activity, commodity extraction, and large-scale construction projects.
Unlike the ubiquitous dry container market, open top containers serve a discrete, project-oriented clientele, making demand more volatile but also offering higher value per unit. The market is characterized by a concentrated manufacturing base, a growing leasing and rental ecosystem, and increasing digitalization in booking and fleet management. Key demand drivers include global infrastructure spending, renewable energy projects, and the expansion of heavy industry in Asia-Pacific and Latin America. However, restraints such as steel price volatility, trade protectionism, and competition from alternative transport modes may temper growth.
This report provides a data-driven analysis of the market size, segmentation, competitive dynamics, and regional outlook, offering stakeholders a transparent view of the opportunities and challenges through 2035.
The baseline scenario for the global open top container market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates moderate but steady growth, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 3.2%, reaching a market index of 137 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook is underpinned by sustained demand from project cargo, construction, and heavy machinery sectors, particularly in Asia-Pacific and Latin America. The market is expected to benefit from increased infrastructure investment, renewable energy installations, and port expansion projects. However, growth will be uneven across regions and segments.
The 40ft open top container segment is projected to maintain the largest share, driven by its versatility in handling oversized cargo. Leasing and rental services are anticipated to gain prominence as shipping lines and logistics providers seek flexibility amid volatile trade flows. Digital platforms for container booking and management will enhance operational efficiency and transparency, further supporting market expansion. Key risks include fluctuations in steel prices, which directly impact manufacturing costs, and geopolitical tensions that could disrupt trade lanes. Additionally, the shift toward alternative materials and container designs may pose long-term challenges.
Overall, the market is poised for gradual expansion, with opportunities in niche applications such as collapsible open top containers and specialized variants for the energy sector.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Rising global infrastructure investment and construction activity, particularly in emerging economies, driving demand for open top containers to transport oversized machinery and materials.
- Expansion of renewable energy projects, including wind and solar farms, requiring specialized containers for heavy equipment and components.
- Growth in project cargo and heavy-lift shipments, supported by increased capital expenditure in oil and gas, mining, and power generation sectors.
- Increasing trade of agricultural commodities and timber, which often require top-loading containers for efficient handling.
- Digitalization of container booking and fleet management, improving utilization rates and reducing turnaround times, thereby stimulating demand.
- Replacement demand for aging open top container fleets, as older units reach end-of-life and need to be retired.
Potential Growth Constraints
- Volatility in steel prices and raw material costs, which directly affect container manufacturing expenses and leasing rates.
- Trade protectionism and geopolitical tensions disrupting global supply chains and trade lanes, leading to uncertainty in demand.
- Competition from alternative transport modes, such as breakbulk vessels and flat racks, which can handle similar cargo types.
- Environmental regulations targeting emissions and waste, increasing compliance costs for manufacturers and operators.
- Limited availability of skilled labor and maintenance services in certain regions, hindering operational efficiency.
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
End-Use Industry Demand Split (%)
Construction Material Logistics (estimated share: 28%)
The construction sector is a primary end-user of open top containers, utilizing them to transport heavy and oversized materials such as steel beams, precast concrete, and large machinery. As global infrastructure investment accelerates, particularly in Asia-Pacific and Latin America, demand for these containers is expected to rise. The shift toward modular construction and prefabricated components further supports the need for top-loading containers, as they allow efficient loading by crane. Key demand indicators include construction spending, urbanization rates, and government infrastructure budgets. Through 2035, the segment will benefit from megaprojects in transportation, energy, and water management.
However, cyclical downturns in construction activity could pose risks. The trend is toward specialized containers that can handle increasingly larger and heavier components, driving innovation in container design. Current trend: Growing steadily due to global infrastructure spending.
Major trends: Increasing use of modular construction methods, Government infrastructure stimulus programs, Growth in urbanization and smart city projects, and Rising demand for sustainable building materials.
Representative participants: CIMC, Triton International, Textainer, Seaco Global, and Beacon Intermodal Leasing.
Oversized Machinery Shipping (estimated share: 22%)
Open top containers are essential for shipping oversized machinery, including industrial equipment, generators, and turbines, which cannot fit through standard container doors. The global trade of heavy machinery is driven by industrialization, energy projects, and manufacturing relocation. As companies invest in automation and upgrade facilities, demand for transporting large machinery increases. Key indicators include machinery production, export orders, and capital expenditure in manufacturing.
