articles.title: 2 Iranian men charged over alleged bomb plot to target UK Jewish community appear in court - CNN
articles.summary: 2 Iranian men charged over alleged bomb plot to target UK Jewish community appear in court  CNNU.K. police accuse 2 Iranian men of planning terror attack on Manchester's Jewish community  CBS NewsProsecutor says 2 Iranian men scouted a UK synagogue for a chlorine bomb plot  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and VideosHomemade bomb part of alleged plot on Manchester's Jewish community, court told  BBCTwo Iranian nationals charged over alleged terrorism ...
articles.full_text:
Two Iranian men charged with terror offenses over an alleged bomb plot to attack the Jewish community in Manchester, England, appeared in a British court on Saturday.
The suspects – named as Salam Ahmadyan, 36, and Rahman Salehi, 34 – were arrested on September 20, on the eve of the Jewish holiday Yom Kippur and almost exactly a year after a terrorist attack at a Manchester synagogue killed two worshippers.
In court on Saturday, prosecutor Mark Luckett alleged that the two men were in contact with an Iranian national, most likely operating from within Iran.
That third party “is alleged to have directed and coordinated the planned attack and provided instructions on how to assemble a homemade explosive device,” Luckett said, according to UK news agency PA Media.
Prosecutors accused the two men of planning and acquiring the elements to make a chlorine bomb as well as using the internet to identify and research potential targets.
The two men allegedly “carried out a hostile reconnaissance within Manchester’s Jewish community, identifying attempted targets such as the Jewish Museum and Heaton Park Synagogue,” Luckett added, referencing the same synagogue hit in the deadly attack last year.
The suspects’ arrest comes after a string of antisemitic attacks this year, including a knife attack in north London and assaults on synagogues and other communal buildings, that have left the country’s Jewish community in a heightened state of fear.
“We continue to see antisemitic sentiment appearing with increasing frequency,” Laurence Taylor, the head of counter-terrorism policing, said Friday in a statement marking a year after the Manchester synagogue attack.
Just days before the Iranian suspects were charged in this case, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham also alleged there were “strong indications” Iran “played a part” in a separate incident which saw six men arrested and bailed over an alleged plot to target a UK airbase used by US forces.
Police emphasized that the foiled attack in Manchester and the incident at the airbase RAF Fairford “are not connected in any way,” even though the week “brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran.”
Several high-level Iranian officials, including Foreign Minister Abbas Aragchi, have categorically denied their country’s involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.
The two defendants in the Manchester case spoke in court through interpreters, only to confirm their names, dates of birth and addresses, PA reported.
Both had arrived in the UK via small boats crossing the English Channel, the court heard, according to PA. These small boat crossings, a notoriously dangerous migration route, have become a political flashpoint in recent years. They have driven harder-line immigration policies from both the center-right Conservative and center-left Labour governments, as well as contributing to the rise of the populist hard-right party Reform UK.
Salehi, who was granted asylum in 2023, had been given the right to remain in the country until July 2028, while Ahmadyan has a pending asylum claim, the court heard, according to PA.
Both suspects will be remanded in custody and next appear in court for a hearing on October 23.
CNN’s Hira Humayun contributed reporting.

articles.title: Pakistan’s LNG Paradox: When An Energy Fix Became An Economic Liability - thefridaytimes.com
articles.summary: Pakistan’s LNG Paradox: When An Energy Fix Became An Economic Liability  thefridaytimes.com
articles.full_text:
Pakistan’s energy economy is caught in an unusual contradiction. On one hand, the country has had more liquefied natural gas (LNG) than it could use, forcing it to divert contracted cargoes to other markets. On the other, when the 2026 Middle East conflict disrupted LNG supplies, Pakistan had to worry about shortages and look again towards the expensive global spot market. At the same time, the gas sector’s circular debt has reached around Rs3.3 trillion, with the costs eventually spreading across the wider economy through higher energy prices, pressure on public finances and losses within state-owned companies.
So how did a fuel once introduced as part of the solution to Pakistan’s energy crisis become such a significant economic burden?
A new report offers an important starting point. On October 1, 2026, Recourse, Africa Change Lab and The Big Shift Global released Gas Is Bad Economics for the Global South, examining the economics of fossil gas in five developing countries, including Pakistan. Its central argument is that countries investing heavily in gas as a “bridge fuel” towards cleaner energy can become locked into debt, volatile international prices and infrastructure that may become less useful as energy markets change. Pakistan provides an important case study of that argument.
A Solution For A Time Of Shortage
Between 2014 and 2016, Pakistan developed infrastructure and long-term arrangements to import LNG. There was a clear reason for doing so. Domestic gas production was declining, industries were struggling with shortages, and prolonged power cuts were hurting businesses and households. Imported LNG offered a relatively quick way to supply fuel to power plants, reduce dependence on expensive furnace oil and provide gas to industry. But the underlying challenge was and remains — energy access. For households and businesses, access means more than having an electricity or gas connection. Energy must also be reliable and affordable. An imported-fuel system therefore cannot be judged only by how much energy it brings into the country, but also by whether its costs help expand affordable and dependable access.
It would be unfair to judge decisions made a decade ago entirely with the benefit of hindsight. Policymakers in 2015 could not have known how quickly solar technology would become cheaper or precisely how Pakistan’s electricity demand would change. The more important question is whether the country’s long-term energy arrangements were flexible enough to adapt when prices, technology and demand changed. Today, that question is worth billions of dollars.
A March 2026 study by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) found that Pakistan had to make arrangements to divert about 45 surplus LNG cargoes contracted from Qatar and Italy’s ENI to other markets. Based on projections by Pakistan’s Petroleum Division, IEEFA estimates that, if the mismatch between demand and contracted supply is not addressed, Pakistan could face as many as 177 surplus cargoes through 2032, with a potential liability of about $5.6 billion, or more if oil prices rise. This is a projection of financial risk rather than a loss Pakistan has already incurred, but it illustrates how expensive long-term contracts can become when the assumptions behind them change.
Then Came The Solar Revolution
While Pakistan remained tied to long-term gas arrangements, consumers were changing the energy market themselves. As grid electricity became more expensive and solar panels became cheaper, households, shops, factories and farmers increasingly began producing their own electricity. IEEFA estimates that Pakistan’s distributed solar capacity reached around 34 gigawatts in 2025, including grid-connected and off-grid systems. Meanwhile, electricity demand from the national grid in fiscal year 2025 was almost 11 per cent lower than in fiscal year 2022. Solar was not the only factor: high electricity prices, weaker industrial demand and slow economic growth also contributed. But solar has clearly become an important part of Pakistan’s changing electricity market.
The change has reached the gas market. Pakistan’s LNG consumption fell by around 1.21 million tonnes in 2025. According to IEEFA, LNG-based electricity generation declined by about 4.5 terawatt-hours, while industrial gas demand also weakened. This creates a difficult economic situation. Consumers reduce their dependence on expensive grid electricity by installing solar panels, lowering demand for some gas-fired generation. The country consequently needs less imported gas. Yet long-term LNG contracts do not automatically adjust when demand falls. Pakistan’s contracts have included “take-or-pay” commitments, under which buyers carry payment obligations for contracted supplies even when demand is weaker, subject to the flexibility provisions of individual agreements. Such arrangements can provide supply security when demand is high, but they reduce flexibility when consumption falls unexpectedly. Pakistan’s LNG surplus therefore exposes a fundamental mismatch: energy demand can change much faster than long-term contractual commitments.
How Can Pakistan Have Too Much Gas And Too Little?
The contradiction became even clearer during the 2026 Middle East conflict. Before the crisis, Pakistan was trying to manage surplus LNG. When regional supply routes were disrupted, however, the country suddenly faced another problem: securing enough gas during periods of high demand. Pakistan introduced an emergency gas management plan and again had to consider buying LNG from the international spot market.
Solar power and a more diverse electricity mix helped the national grid cope with reduced LNG availability. But solar does not produce electricity at night, meaning gas and other dependable sources were still required to meet peak evening demand. This highlights an important aspect of energy security. It is not simply about signing contracts to buy more fuel. Pakistan has long-term LNG contracts but very limited capacity to store LNG. When demand is low, surplus gas creates pressure on the system; when international supply is suddenly disrupted, the same country can face shortages. Surplus and shortage are therefore not necessarily opposites. In Pakistan’s case, they can be two symptoms of the same problem: an energy system that does not have enough flexibility.
When Imported Gas Pushed Out Cheaper Local Gas
Perhaps one of the most striking examples came in 2025. Pakistan had too much gas in its pipeline system and insufficient storage capacity, causing pipeline pressure to rise. To manage the problem, the government had to reduce production from domestic gas fields by around 270 to 400 million cubic feet per day. IEEFA reports that state-owned Oil and Gas Development Company suffered around Rs43 billion in revenue losses as a result.
The economics are difficult to ignore. According to the IEEFA analysis, imported LNG was roughly three times as expensive as domestic gas. Yet contractual obligations and limited storage meant that, at times, Pakistan had to reduce production of cheaper domestic gas while imported LNG remained in the system. At that point, the problem was no longer simply the international price of LNG. The structure of the system itself was creating additional costs.
 Pakistan’s LNG surplus and recurring gas shortages are not necessarily opposites; they can be two symptoms of the same problem — an energy system that lacks the flexibility to respond to changing demand and supply.
The Rs3.3 Trillion Question
Pakistan’s gas-sector circular debt adds another layer to the problem. By early 2026, it stood at around Rs3.3 trillion. It would be wrong to attribute all of this debt to LNG. The problem has multiple causes, including differences between the actual cost of gas and prices charged to some consumers, subsidies, unpaid bills, old liabilities, theft, pipeline leakage and problems with measurement and recovery. But expensive imported gas makes these weaknesses more costly. IEEFA estimates that unaccounted-for gas losses are around 11.7 per cent. This can include technical leakage, theft, metering problems and other losses. Not all of this can simply be described as poor management, since gas networks inevitably experience some technical losses. Nevertheless, reducing leakage, controlling theft, improving metering and recovering bills remain basic responsibilities of gas companies and regulators.
This matters directly to ordinary consumers. If Pakistan imports expensive gas, fails to recover all its costs, loses a significant amount within the system and then responds by increasing tariffs, consumers are not paying only for the international price of gas. They can also end up carrying part of the cost of weaknesses within the domestic system. The government therefore needs to distinguish between the different sources of the financial gap: imported fuel, subsidies, unpaid bills, old liabilities and losses within gas companies. Without that separation, higher tariffs risk becoming a substitute for better management.
The Role Of International Finance
Pakistan’s LNG system was not built with domestic resources alone. International financial institutions helped finance parts of the infrastructure. The International Finance Corporation and the Asian Development Bank participated in financing Pakistan’s first major LNG terminal, while other institutions supported gas transmission, energy-sector reforms and fuel imports. At the time, the logic was understandable. Pakistan urgently needed energy, and LNG appeared to offer a faster alternative to shortages and expensive liquid fuels. But development finance cannot be judged only by whether a project was successfully built. Energy markets, technology and demand change, and the long-term economics of earlier investments need to be reassessed when they do.

articles.summary: Why The Recent Crude Oil Tanker Strike Off Oman Should Worry Global Shipping  ИФЗ РАН
articles.full_text:
Commercial shipping lanes in the Middle East are flashing red again. A crude oil tanker recently took a direct hit from an unknown projectile just four nautical miles east of Oman, triggering immediate safety alarms across the international maritime community. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations confirmed that the vessel's port side took the impact, though thankfully, all crew members walked away uninjured and no oil spills hit the water.
If you are following global energy corridors, this isn't an isolated accident. It is part of a dangerous escalation pattern threatening vital commercial lifelines.
The Reality of Middle East Maritime Risks
When a crude oil tanker gets struck near the Strait of Hormuz or Omani waters, the shockwaves hit global energy markets immediately. Shippers can't afford complacency. Regional tensions have turned vital chokepoints into high-risk zones where vessels operate under constant threat.
Just before this latest strike off Oman, five Indian nationals aboard the Kuwait-flagged tanker MT Kazimah III had to be frantically rescued and shifted ashore after their ship took a projectile hit in the Strait of Hormuz. The Embassy of India in Oman coordinated that rescue, highlighting the very real dangers faced by thousands of civilian mariners every day.
Right now, numbers from the Ministry of External Affairs show thousands of Indian seafarers working across active commercial cargo ships in the Persian Gulf. When incidents happen, it's real human lives on the line—not just abstract statistics on a commodity ticker.
Why Shippers and Insurers Are Panicking
Security advisories issued by bodies like the UKMTO aren't just bureaucratic paperwork. They dictate multimillion-dollar logistics decisions. When a ship reports an unknown projectile hitting its hull, marine insurers immediately reevaluate risk premiums.
- War risk insurance spikes overnight.
- Charterers hesitate to send crews through high-threat corridors.
- Rerouting around dangerous zones adds days to transit times and burns extra fuel.
We've seen this movie before. Commercial shipping has faced recurring attacks across the Red Sea, the Persian Gulf, and the Black Sea. Each incident tightens the operational bottleneck for global oil supply chains.
What Happens Next for Seafarer Safety
Governments and shipping companies are scrambling to protect their fleets, but defense measures can't cover every single mile of open ocean. While the Omani authorities and local coast guards investigate the source of this latest projectile, commercial vessels are told to transit with extreme caution and report any suspicious activity instantly.
If you manage logistics or track global commodity flows, stop viewing these security alerts as background noise. They are direct indicators of how fragile current maritime trade routes actually are. Keep a close eye on insurance rate adjustments and rerouting announcements over the coming weeks.

articles.title: Why the Iran War Equation is Changing, and Why a Third War May be Closer Than It Seems - Countercurrents.org
articles.summary: Why the Iran War Equation is Changing, and Why a Third War May be Closer Than It Seems  Countercurrents.org
articles.full_text:
It appears that the main actors involved in the previous 40-day war are increasingly moving toward another confrontation for their own reasons. The regional equation has changed significantly in recent weeks, and that change is making the continuation of the current ceasefire less attractive. Iran is under growing economic pressure because it cannot export its oil normally. The Houthis have moved closer to controlling the approaches to Bab el-Mandeb. Israel is approaching an important election. And the United States is facing a decision over whether to continue the current stalemate or return to major military operations.
The argument here is simple: when the equation changes, the policies that made sense under the previous equation may stop making sense. The longer the new conditions continue, the stronger the incentives for the main actors to change them.
Iran Has an Incentive to Break the Siege
Iran’s most immediate problem is economic. The US-led naval blockade and the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz have sharply to sell and export oil. in September Iran was facing one of the most severe economic crises in its history, with the blockade and sanctions causing shortages of foreign currency, declining imports and rising prices. Trump has also said that the blockade has prevented Iranian oil exports.
For Iran, the calculation is straightforward. If Iran cannot sell its oil, it cannot maintain normal economic activity. If the blockade continues, the economic cost will continue to rise. Therefore, Tehran has an increasing reason to change the situation rather than simply continue under the same conditions.
A political agreement could restore oil exports and reduce the pressure. But if negotiations fail, Iran could also consider military action to break the blockade and reopen its export routes. That does not mean Iran has decided to start another war. It means that the economic situation is creating a direct incentive to take stronger action. If military force becomes the chosen way to break the siege, the result could be a new phase of war.
Bab el-Mandeb Is Creating a Second Front
The biggest change in the regional equation, however, may be taking place in Yemen. The Houthis have recently expanded along Yemen’s Red Sea coast. They captured Mocha and then moved toward the islands around Bab el-Mandeb. On September 11, Houthi forces , or Mayun, Island in the strait, after government forces withdrew. Other reports said the group had also reached the Hanish islands. These positions are important because Bab el-Mandeb is a major shipping route connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
This matters because Iran already has leverage over the Strait of Hormuz. If the Houthis consolidate their positions around Bab el-Mandeb, an Iran-aligned force could also threaten the second major maritime route linking Middle Eastern energy producers to global markets.
That would change the strategic calculation for every major actor in the region. Saudi Arabia is particularly exposed. Its East-West pipeline normally allows it to move oil from the eastern fields to Yanbu on the Red Sea, bypassing Hormuz. But on September 13 had shut the pipeline, which can carry around four million barrels per day. Saudi oil production had also fallen sharply, while available stocks at Yanbu were limited.
Saudi Arabia is therefore losing some of its ability to bypass the crisis. If Hormuz remains heavily disrupted while Bab el-Mandeb becomes another pressure point, the ability of Gulf producers to move oil to international markets becomes much more vulnerable. For the Houthis, this creates an opportunity to increase their leverage. For Iran, it creates a potentially valuable second pressure point. For Saudi Arabia, Israel and the United States, it creates a reason to prevent the new situation from becoming permanent.
Brent crude has already moved above , while oil flows through Hormuz remain below normal levels. If both Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb were simultaneously subjected to serious military pressure, the effect on oil markets would be much larger than the disruption of either route alone.
Israel and the United States Also Have Reasons to Act
The third change is political. Israel’s national election is scheduled for October 27. shows a highly competitive race, with no clear path for either major bloc to form a government. Reuters reported that the opposition bloc was ahead in polling averages, although the final political balance remains uncertain.
The election does not mean that Israel will choose war, but it creates a deadline. If the Israeli government believes that the regional balance is changing against it, waiting may become less attractive. A government facing an election has a reason to consider whether it should change the strategic situation before the political environment changes.
The United States faces a similar problem, although for different reasons.
President Donald Trump said on September 17 that he was approaching a “big decision” over whether to resume major attacks on Iran. Trump has also said that he hopes the war is nearing its end, but his latest comments show that a return to major military operations remains under consideration. Washington therefore has two reasons to reconsider the current situation: continuing the war is costly, while waiting gives Iran and the Houthis more time to strengthen their positions.
This is the central point of the changing war equation. Iran has a growing reason to break the economic blockade. The Houthis have a reason to consolidate their gains around Bab el-Mandeb. Saudi Arabia has a reason to restore secure oil-export routes. Israel has a political deadline and a reason to prevent further deterioration of its strategic position. And the United States has to decide whether the current stalemate is preferable to another military operation.
The actors are not simply waiting for the previous war to end. They are responding to a new set of conditions, and those conditions are giving them new reasons to change the status quo. The danger is not that another war could begin without anyone having a reason to fight. The opposite is true. Several actors now have their own reasons to change the current situation, and some of those reasons directly conflict with the interests of the others. As the equation continues to change, maintaining the status quo becomes harder. That is what makes a third war more plausible than it appeared only a few weeks ago.

articles.title: What is Oman’s relationship with Israel – if any? - Jewish Telegraphic Agency
articles.summary: What is Oman’s relationship with Israel – if any?  Jewish Telegraphic Agency
articles.full_text:
TEL AVIV – The Omani pilot who allegedly tried to hijack and crash a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv has drawn new attention to his native country. Oman, which has sometimes been dubbed the “Switzerland of the Middle East,” has long sought to balance its relations with the West and Iran. Its strategic location, combined with its distinctive diplomatic approach, has made it an unusual player in the Middle East.
Oman is located on the southeastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, bordering Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen. It sits alongside the Strait of Hormuz, the strategically important maritime passage through which roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil supply passes.
Until recently, Oman wasn’t a Middle Eastern country used to finding itself in international headlines. But it has emerged as a key player in recent months after long serving as a central mediator between Washington and Tehran. Its neutral posture, along with its close ties to both the United States and Iran, placed it in an important position during the talks between the two sides before the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war earlier this year.
When Omani mediation failed to prevent the conflict, Oman condemned the joint U.S.-Israeli military campaign launched in February, saying it had “deep regrets at the military operations launched by Israel and the United States of America against the Islamic Republic of Iran” and that it “considers this action to be in contravention of the rules of international law.”
Even after Iran itself attacked Oman, which hosts three U.S. military bases, as part of Tehran’s campaign to pressure countries in the region and deter President Donald Trump, Muscat did not abandon its neutral stance. The targets Iran struck in Oman included a port and oil infrastructure, although the attacks were limited compared with those on other countries in the region.
Relations between Washington and Muscat have become further strained as the war has continued. In an opinion article published in The Economist, Oman’s foreign minister described the war as “unlawful” and said the United States “has lost control of its foreign policy.”
Trump, meanwhile, threatened to bomb Oman, telling reporters in August, “I don’t think they behaved very well, but we’d handle them very easily just like we do others.” The Wall Street Journal reported that senior U.S. officials had privately accused Oman of being “a duplicitous actor” that largely sides with Iran rather than seeking the best possible deal between Washington and Tehran.
While the Gulf state maintains significant ties with Washington, it does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel. The two countries once maintained commercial relations, but those ties were cut in 2000 amid a deterioration in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Contacts between the countries later continued quietly, and Netanyahu visited Oman in 2018 in a rare public meeting between an Israeli prime minister and an Omani sultan.
The two countries have held discussions about establishing formal relations, but those efforts have not come to fruition to date. Oman’s position has remained broadly similar to that of Saudi Arabia, which talked openly about the possibility of normalization with Israel but has conditioned that recognition on a clear, irreversible path toward a Palestinian state. Oman has also expressed support for the Abraham Accords, which normalized relations between Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain in 2020 and have since been signed by a handful of other Muslim countries.
Oman’s rhetoric toward Israel has grown harsher since Oct. 7, 2023, and relations between the countries have cooled. Omani officials have strongly criticized Israel’s conduct in Gaza and have been particularly critical of Israel’s war against Iran.
Ahmed bin Hamad al-Khalili, Oman’s grand mufti, described Israel’s attack on Iran as “treacherous American-Zionist aggression against Iran.”
A strategic Gulf state
Much of Oman’s geographic importance comes from its position along bodies of water through which large quantities of oil transit. Its land, in contrast, is covered by desert alongside a coastal plain that is home to a significant share of the country’s population of roughly 5.5 million.
That population is distinctive in the Muslim world: A significant portion of its citizens belong to the Ibadi branch of Islam, a tradition separate from both Sunni and Shiite Islam. The country is also home to a large expatriate population made up of people from different religious backgrounds.
Oman is a sultanate, meaning the sultan holds extensive powers. The current ruler, Sultan Haitham bin Tarik Al Said, took office in January 2020 following the death of his cousin, Sultan Qaboos, who had ruled the country for nearly 50 years.
A significant part of Oman’s economy is based on oil, although the country has sought to diversify its economy. Its strategic location and extensive coastline have also made it a gateway for international trade between Europe and Asia.
Oman has so far not issued an official response to the incident or publicly confirmed the identity or nationality of the pilot who allegedly carried out the flydubai attack. But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and international media outlets have described the pilot as Omani.
In a statement, Netanyahu said that “the perpetrator underwent Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane. We are now investigating whether he was sent, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price.”

Wednesday’s flydubai saga crammed the new Middle East into a single aircraft.
An Emirati airline carrying Israelis made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia amid war with Iran – and the incident was immediately drawn into an Israeli election campaign dominated by the question of who can keep the country safe.
Talk about one event bringing everything together.
But beyond the frightening drama aboard the plane, the incident also brought something else into focus: how much the region has changed, and where the limits of that change still lie.
Israelis were flying home on an Emirati airline. When their flight turned into a nightmare, they landed in Saudi Arabia, received medical attention and assistance, and were eventually collected by another Emirati aircraft and brought to Israel.
For all the tensions, wars, and political sensitivities, that sequence is worth noting. The absence of Saudi-Israeli diplomatic relations did not prevent the passengers from receiving help or getting home.
Granted, the Saudis refused to let an Israeli aircraft collect them. That matters and is maddening, especially considering the security and intelligence cooperation that does exist between the two countries. But it need not obscure what they did allow, or turn a story of regional cooperation into a tale primarily about rejection.
The new Middle East is imperfect. Wednesday showed, however, that it is also real.
A changing Middle East takes shape
TO APPRECIATE the broader picture, connect the dots from earlier in the week.
On Sunday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu flew secretly to Abu Dhabi to meet UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed, known as MBZ.
According to reports, Netanyahu shared intelligence about Iran’s continued nuclear ambitions, including new construction at the deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain site, as well as developments involving the Houthis in the Red Sea.
These are issues on which Israel and the Gulf states have overlapping interests. An Iran rebuilding its nuclear capabilities concerns more than Jerusalem. So do the Houthis threatening Red Sea shipping.
But Netanyahu reportedly brought another concern to the meeting, one rooted in Israel’s election campaign.
AP reported that he asked MBZ to deny the Haaretz account that the Emirati leader had warned him about a looming Hamas threat before October 7.
This report has since mushroomed into several accounts of warnings that Netanyahu allegedly received but did not act on before October 7. And all of this has figured prominently in opposition party attacks on him during the campaign. Netanyahu’s office has denied he received any such warning.
The visit thus carried two possible purposes: discussing threats facing the region now and addressing allegations about what Netanyahu knew back then.
That combination is characteristic of this election campaign. Netanyahu wants the public to focus on what he has done to reshape the region since October 7. His opponents want it to focus on what he failed to prevent on that Simchat Torah morning.
A meeting with an important Arab leader can serve the first argument. Reports that the same leader warned him before the attack feed the second.
The UAE confirmed that Sunday’s meeting took place, unlike in May, when it denied Netanyahu’s claim of an earlier visit. That acknowledgment gave him something to point to: evidence that, despite the wars and international criticism, he could still meet a key Arab leader.
The UAE did not, however, deny that a pre-October 7 call had taken place. Netanyahu came away, therefore, with the proverbial half a loaf: confirmation of Sunday’s meeting, but no denial of the earlier warning.
There were also reports that representatives of other Arab countries attended discussions in Abu Dhabi, including Saudi representatives, though the Saudis denied it.
Then, on Tuesday, MBZ’s brother, UAE Vice President Mansour bin Zayed, traveled to Riyadh and met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman.
With the Houthis again threatening Saudi interests, the two Gulf powers had reason to repair ties ruptured by their competing policies in Yemen.
Might the timing – two days after Netanyahu’s meeting with MBZ – have been a coincidence?
It might. But it also might not.
The sequence raises the possibility of wider coordination against threats that concern Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE alike. It does not, however, establish that Netanyahu brokered the Saudi-Emirati rapprochement, or that all three countries agreed on a common policy.
There is enough here to connect some dots. There is not enough to color in the entire picture.
Still, the meetings suggest a region in which governments have reasons to work through their differences because the threats facing them are greater than those differences.
THEN THE flydubai flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai for Tel Aviv.
That flight is the stuff of movies: one pilot stabs another and tries to crash the aircraft before passengers, along with a crew member, intervene and save the day. The plane makes an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Passengers later describe receiving medical attention and assistance there.
For those aboard, this was a terrifying brush with catastrophe. Their survival owed much to the people who intervened and helped bring the aircraft down safely.
What happened next carried its own regional significance: a plane carrying Israelis lands in Saudi Arabia, its passengers receive help, and the UAE sends another aircraft to bring them home.
Each part of that sequence may seem practical and unremarkable on its own. Taken together, however, they describe a regional reality that Israelis should not take for granted.
And that is precisely one of the main achievements of the Abraham Accords: making previously extraordinary things – like a flight from the East on an Arab airline over Saudi Arabia – ordinary.
That does not make Saudi Arabia a party to the Abraham Accords. But it does show that the relationships created by the accords can function in a wider regional setting, even where formal diplomatic ties are absent.
The Saudis nevertheless drew a line, rejecting Israel’s request to send a plane to collect the passengers. Another flydubai plane eventually brought them back home.
That refusal understandably irked Israelis who felt that, after what the passengers had endured, getting them home on an Israeli plane so they felt safe should have overridden political considerations.
Tellingly, Netanyahu chose to stress the Saudi willingness to receive the plane and the hospitality shown to its passengers.
Just a week ago at the UN, he chose to call out by name the leaders of France and Turkey whose words and actions harm the Jewish State, proving he is not shy about doing so when he deems it necessary or politically expedient. He didn’t do so with Saudi Arabia.
There was a practical reason for that restraint: publicly berating the Saudis would hardly strengthen the cooperation that already exists and benefits both sides.
There was also a political reason: Netanyahu has an interest in presenting the region as one in which Israel’s relationships have expanded, even if full normalization with Riyadh remains elusive.
In this case, emphasizing the cooperation also reflected an important part of what happened. The assistance the Saudis did provide showed that the lack of diplomatic relations need not prevent practical help.
But the Saudi refusal to allow Israel to send a plane to retrieve the passengers showed how carefully Riyadh guards the boundary between basic humanitarian help – allowing the plane to land – and a visible gesture toward Israel.
Perhaps the approaching election made the Saudis especially reluctant to allow a scene that Netanyahu could then use in his campaign. An Israeli aircraft retrieving passengers from Saudi soil would have made a striking picture.
It would be a stretch, however, to assume that everything becomes easier after October 27. Saudi reservations about public normalization extend far beyond a reluctance to give Netanyahu a campaign gift.
The limits of regional normalization
THE ATTEMPTED hijacking has also been framed as a test of Israel-UAE ties and the staying power of the Abraham Accords.
That is understandable since the Tel Aviv-Dubai air routes are the accords’ most visible, tangible benefits for the average Israeli. A terrifying incident can shake public confidence in flying that route, and passengers will now understandably want to know what is being done to prevent a recurrence.
But the Israel-UAE relationship will certainly withstand this shock. A relationship that has endured October 7 and wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran rests on interests that one attempted hijacking will not shake. If anything, the incident shows the threats both countries face, why they need each other, and how they can help one another.
The regional lesson is broader.
The Saudi refusal showed that significant political barriers to normalization remain, and that Riyadh still insists on keeping its relationship with Israel in the back room rather than bringing it into the front room.
The passengers’ safe return showed, however, that even a relationship confined to the back room can produce practical cooperation when it matters.
The Abraham Accords did not produce a Middle East free of hostility, danger, or diplomatic sensitivities. They did, however, help create a region where Israelis forced to land in an Arab country can receive assistance rather than face unbridled hostility.
Wednesday was a nightmare for the passengers and their families. For the region, however, the response offered something encouraging: evidence that the relationships built up in recent years can deliver practical help when it is needed most.

articles.title: War Under the Ceiling: How Have the Rules of Engagement Changed Between Israel, Palestine, Lebanon, and Syria? - صوت الإمارات
articles.summary: War Under the Ceiling: How Have the Rules of Engagement Changed Between Israel, Palestine, Lebanon, and Syria?  صوت الإمارات

Abu Dhabi, UAE – Where does the war end and a settlement begin in the Middle East? It is a question difficult to answer if we rely solely on maps of bombardment and lines of contact; the landscape stretching from Gaza to southern Lebanon and southern Syria reveals a far more complex reality: ceasefires that fail to halt military operations, conditional withdrawals that are deferred, security zones that expand or contract, and political communications unfolding in parallel with developments on the ground.
While the four fronts may appear distinct on a map, their threads converge on a shared set of questions: Who determines the depth of the “safe zone”? Who holds the decision to escalate or de-escalate? And what prevents a strike in Gaza, Lebanon, or Syria from igniting another front? A review of recent developments on the ground and in the political arena reveals a shift in the conflict from open warfare to a more complex equation—one in which armies, factions, and mediators operate within a gray zone between war and peace, where a temporary measure risks becoming a permanent reality.
Gaza: Ceasefire Amidst Strikes and Disarmament
Despite the ongoing ceasefire framework in Gaza, violence has not ceased entirely; recent strikes by Israel have been recorded within the Strip, while Israel and the factions have traded accusations regarding responsibility for the continued tension. On October 1, Palestinian sources reported that one Palestinian was killed and another injured in a drone strike, amidst ongoing debate over the extent of actual adherence to the ceasefire.
The issue of disarming Hamas remains at the heart of the negotiations, following Washington’s announcement of plans to end the war in stages, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has insisted that an Israeli withdrawal will not take place until the movement is disarmed. Consequently, the transition from a truce to a settlement has become linked to two intertwined issues: who holds the weapons within Gaza, and who holds the decision-making power regarding an Israeli withdrawal from the Strip.
Southern Lebanon: Land for Weapons
In southern Lebanon, areas under Israeli control have become a focal point of the political and security confrontation. In June, Israel announced a map outlining an expanded military control zone in the south—amid ongoing talk of potential strikes beyond that perimeter—while Beirut maintained its demand for the recovery of its entire territory.
Israel conditions withdrawal on security guarantees, the removal of Hezbollah from the border, and the disarming of the group; meanwhile, Hezbollah refuses to discuss its weaponry prior to the end of the Israeli presence, according to reports on the negotiations. Consequently, southern Lebanon faces a complex equation: Israeli withdrawal is linked to security arrangements, and security arrangements are linked to Hezbollah’s weapons, all while the Lebanese Army faces the task of expanding its presence in the south.
Syria and Israel: Southern Syria at the Heart of New Calculations
Southern Syria represents one of the most sensitive conflict zones following the political transformations the country has undergone since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in 2024. Israel views the areas near the Golan as a sensitive security zone, while Damascus faces the challenge of rebuilding state institutions, securing borders, and managing relations with the armed forces that were active within Syrian territory.
At the same time, signs emerged of a shift in the nature of the relationship between Damascus and Hezbollah. On October 1, Reuters published a report—citing six sources—regarding an alleged secret meeting in Turkey during September between Syrian officials and Hezbollah representatives. According to the sources, the meeting addressed easing tensions, halting arms smuggling, and dismantling Hezbollah cells within Syria. However, both Damascus and Ankara denied that the meeting took place, and no official confirmation was issued, leaving the details of the encounter officially unverified.
Hezbollah and Syria: Redrawing the Cross-Border Relationship
The account published by Reuters—despite official denials—raises a broader question regarding the future of the relationship between Damascus and Hezbollah following the fall of Assad. The party was a fundamental part of the Syrian equation throughout the war years, whereas the current Syrian government seeks to reassert control over the borders and prevent Syrian territory from being used for armed activities or smuggling operations.
According to the sources quoted by Reuters, the alleged contacts focused on security files, including weapons smuggling and the presence of cells affiliated with the party inside Syria, while discussing mutual guarantees related to non-military intervention. But the Syrian and Turkish denials prevent these details from being treated as an official agreement or understanding, and make what has been confirmed so far is the continued rearrangement of security relations in the region, and not the existence of an announced deal between Damascus and Hezbollah.
Israel: From Military Response to Security Zones
Over the past few months, Israel has moved to establish a military presence or create security zones along the periphery of certain fronts, viewing the distancing of threats from its borders as part of the effort to protect its citizens. In southern Lebanon, Reuters reports have pointed to a buffer zone within Lebanese territory, while in June, Israel released a map showing an expanded military control zone in the south.
This development marks a shift in the nature of military operations; rather than merely responding after attacks occur, controlling areas near the border has become part of security calculations. Conversely, Lebanese parties view the continued Israeli presence within Lebanese territory as an obstacle to restoring full sovereignty, thereby making the border areas themselves a subject of negotiation rather than simply a theater for military operations.
Why did the four fronts not merge into a single war?
Despite the geographical and political interconnections linking Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, and Israel, the trajectories of escalation continue to unfold at varying intensities. In Gaza, negotiations are underway regarding disarmament and withdrawal; in Lebanon, discussions are proceeding concerning security arrangements and Hezbollah’s weaponry; meanwhile, Syria is navigating a new regional landscape where issues of borders, the Israeli presence, and relations with armed factions intersect.
These developments indicate that the military track is operating in parallel with the political track, rather than serving as a substitute for it. Military strikes do not necessarily signify the collapse of negotiation channels, nor do negotiations imply a halt to military operations; this explains the persistence of a situation that falls somewhere between open warfare and stable calm.
The United States: Managing Escalation Across Multiple Tracks
Washington plays a pivotal role in attempting to manage the trajectory of the conflict, particularly in Gaza and Lebanon. Regarding Gaza, the US administration has pushed for a plan centered on a phased end to the war—linked to the disarmament of Hamas and an Israeli withdrawal—while Egypt, Qatar, and Turkey have participated in mediation efforts.
In Lebanon, diplomatic efforts have focused on a formula combining an Israeli withdrawal, the deployment of the Lebanese Army, and the disarmament of Hezbollah. However, conflicting demands among the parties remain the primary obstacle: Israel insists on security guarantees prior to withdrawal, whereas Hezbollah refuses to make concessions regarding its arsenal while the Israeli presence persists. Consequently, Washington faces the task of managing simultaneous disputes rather than possessing a single solution for all four fronts.
Israeli elections add a political dimension to the conflict.
Ongoing regional tensions coincide with Israel’s preparations for the elections scheduled for October 27, 2026, adding a domestic dimension to the debate over war management, security, and the military presence along the borders. Netanyahu’s recent address to the UN General Assembly demonstrated a clear focus on security issues and regional threats, coinciding with his election campaign.
This does not mean that military developments can be explained solely by the elections, as they are also linked to security, operational, and negotiating considerations. However, the approaching vote turns the issues of Gaza, Lebanon, and regional threats into part of the domestic political debate—particularly given the ongoing disagreement regarding the nature of an Israeli withdrawal and the parameters of future security arrangements.
From Lines of Fire to Lines of Influence
Developments across the four fronts reveal a gradual shift in the nature of the conflict; competition is no longer solely about controlling cities or altering contact lines, but has come to hinge on denying the adversary access to specific areas, determining the depth of military deployment, controlling border corridors, and imposing preconditions for any withdrawal or settlement.
In this equation, border regions become bargaining chips just as much as they are military battlegrounds. Pentagon Confirms Third Carrier Deployment
The United States Department of Defense is actively preparing to deploy a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, marking a significant escalation in the region's already volatile security landscape. This strategic military maneuver involves the mobilization of approximately 10,000 additional troops, alongside advanced naval assets designed to project power and deter potential adversaries. The deployment comes at a critical juncture, as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue to simmer over nuclear ambitions and regional proxy conflicts. Military analysts suggest that the presence of three carrier strike groups simultaneously in the Middle East provides the Pentagon with unprecedented operational flexibility, enabling sustained air campaigns, enhanced missile defense capabilities, and rapid response options. The sheer scale of this buildup underscores the seriousness with which the US government views the current geopolitical threats, signaling a robust commitment to protecting its allies and securing vital maritime chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz.
Strategic Implications for the Region
The strategic implications of this deployment extend far beyond mere military posturing, as it fundamentally alters the balance of power in the Gulf region. Regional allies, including Israel and Saudi Arabia, have reportedly welcomed the increased American presence, viewing it as a necessary counterweight to Iranian influence and a guarantee of their national security. Conversely, Tehran has condemned the move as a provocative act of aggression, warning that any hostile actions would be met with swift and decisive retaliation. The concentration of such formidable naval firepower in a relatively confined geographic area also raises concerns about the potential for miscalculation or accidental escalation, particularly given the frequent close encounters between US and Iranian naval vessels in the Persian Gulf. Diplomatic channels remain open, but the prevailing atmosphere is one of heightened suspicion and mutual distrust, with both sides engaging in aggressive rhetoric and military exercises designed to signal resolve and deterrence.
Political Context and Midterm Timing
Political analysts note that the timing of this significant military escalation coincides closely with the post-midterm election period in the United States, suggesting that domestic political considerations may be influencing the administration's foreign policy calculus. With the midterm elections now behind them, the current administration appears to be adopting a more assertive stance on the global stage, seeking to demonstrate strength and resolve to both domestic constituents and international partners. The decision to deploy additional troops and naval assets may also be intended to reassure skeptical allies who have questioned the reliability of American security guarantees in recent years. Furthermore, the buildup serves as a powerful bargaining chip in any potential future negotiations with Iran, providing the US with significant leverage should diplomatic efforts resume. However, critics argue that such aggressive military posturing risks entangling the United States in another protracted Middle Eastern conflict, diverting resources and attention from other pressing global priorities.
Logistical and Financial Scale
The logistical complexity of deploying and sustaining a third carrier strike group, along with 10,000 additional personnel, cannot be overstated. It requires a massive coordinated effort involving the Military Sealift Command, the Air Force, and various allied nations to ensure the continuous flow of supplies, ammunition, and fuel to the forward-deployed forces. The establishment of temporary bases, the expansion of existing facilities, and the integration of new command and control structures are all critical components of this operation. Moreover, the financial cost of such a deployment is astronomical, running into billions of dollars, which has inevitably sparked debate among lawmakers regarding the sustainability of such an expansive military footprint. Despite these challenges, the Pentagon maintains that the strategic benefits of maintaining a robust deterrent presence in the Middle East far outweigh the financial and logistical burdens, arguing that the cost of inaction could be far greater in terms of regional instability and global economic disruption.
Global Repercussions and Energy Markets
As the deployment unfolds, the international community watches closely, aware that the decisions made in the coming weeks could have profound and lasting consequences for global security. The United Nations and various international mediation bodies have called for restraint and dialogue, urging all parties to avoid actions that could further inflame the situation. Meanwhile, global energy markets remain on edge, with oil prices fluctuating in response to every development in the Gulf. The potential disruption to global oil supplies, should a conflict erupt, would have severe repercussions for the global economy, particularly for energy-importing nations in Europe and Asia. Ultimately, the success of this military buildup will be measured not by the sheer scale of the forces deployed, but by its ability to deter conflict and create the conditions for a sustainable diplomatic resolution. The coming months will be a critical test of statecraft, military strategy, and the enduring quest for stability in one of the world's most volatile regions.

articles.title: Trump says Iran "ready to fold up," after threatening post-midterm attacks - CBS News
articles.summary: Trump says Iran "ready to fold up," after threatening post-midterm attacks  CBS News
articles.full_text:
Follow . See earlier developments below.
What to know about the Iran war:
- President Trump said Thursday night that Iran "is ready to fold up," adding he believes the U.S. will win the war "right after the election," though he also said "maybe before the election."
- Mr. Trump told TIME magazine that U.S. military action against Iran could resume after the midterm elections if Tehran and Washington fail to reach a satisfactory agreement, and that he doesn't think "you could ever have peace" with Iran.
- Mr. Trump told reporters Thursday that Iran might be linked to a a packed plane traveling from Dubai to Israel. The president didn't offer any further details and said Iran would be hit "very hard" if it was determined that Tehran was behind the incident.
Saudi coalition accuses Houthis of drone attack on holy city of Medina
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said Thursday that the Houthis struck an electricity distribution station in the holy city of Medina in Saudi Arabia. The alleged attack sparked strong condemnation from the Muslim world.
It came as fighting intensifies in Yemen, where government forces said they carried out attacks on Houthi targets and AFP journalists heard explosions in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition said the drone struck Medina's Taibah electricity distribution station, which provides power to the Prophet's Mosque, though the Houthis denied involvement.
Medina, the burial place of the Prophet Mohammed and home to the Prophet's Mosque, is one of Islam's holiest cities alongside Mecca.
Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said a drone struck the Taibah electricity distribution station at 5:11 am local time on September 29.
"The investigation and evidence gathered by the competent authorities have confirmed the involvement of the Terrorist Houthi Militia in planning and executing this cowardly terrorist act, based on after-action review and the wreckage of the drone used," he said in a statement.
The coalition said one transformer was taken out of service without affecting the wider electricity network.
CBS/AFP  
Trump says Iran "ready to fold up" and "will be very quickly ended"
Speaking in Denton, Texas, Thursday night at the Peterbilt Motors facility, President Trump said Iran "is ready to fold up."
He said he believes the U.S. will win the war "right after the election," though he also said "maybe before the election."
"I'm ensuring that Iran will be very quickly ended," the president said, adding that energy prices would be "rapidly, rapidly coming" down.
Mr. Trump said the U.S. is "trying to be nice" to the current Iranian leader. "We don't know who the hell to deal with, to be honest with you. Nobody wants to be president," he said.
U.S. naval presence builds in the Middle East as ships deploy
Three ships carrying over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines are heading to the Middle East, a U.S. official told the Associated Press on Thursday.
The group includes the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group.
It could mean three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October, according to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
That would create an unusually high U.S. naval presence of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines and hundreds of aircraft. The USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington are in the area now, along with the USS Boxer amphibious readiness group.
Treasury Department targets shadow banking network used by Iranian regime
The U.S. Treasury Department took "unprecedented action" Thursday targeting a shadow banking network with ties to Russia that the Iranian regime has used to evade sanctions.
The Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network said on X that it had proposed a rule that would prohibit transmittals of funds that involved the A7 Network. The network was also sanctioned as a "significant transnational criminal organization."
An alert was also issued to help financial institutions detect and report suspicious activity related to the A7 Network.
The actions are part of "Operation Economic Outcast," a sustained effort by the Trump administration meant to put financial pressure on Tehran. The U.S. Treasury also issued new sanctions affecting Iran's rail and automobile industries.
Houthi rebels, Yemeni government forces clash in residential areas
Iran-backed Houthi rebels clashed with Yemeni government forces overnight into Thursday in residential neighborhoods in eastern Taiz, located about 60 miles from Mokha, which the Houthis seized last month.
A main road linking Taiz and Aden was cut off due to the latest clashes.
Al-Thawra Hospital, located a few kilometers from the clashes, received six bodies and 35 wounded people Thursday, according to hospital manager Abdelrahman al-Sabry.
The official told The Associated Press by phone Thursday the number of dead and wounded was similar to those in early September, when fighting was intense before clashes de-escalated.
Renewed violence in Yemen has killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands. The Houthis captured the strategic city of Mokha and a number of Red Sea islands last month, extending their reach to the key maritime waterway of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
It was the Houthis' biggest land grab in years and ended a 2022 ceasefire that largely stopped major fighting in Yemen's 12-year civil war.
Trump suggests Iran may be linked to attempted FlyDubai crash
President Trump suggested Thursday that Iran may be linked to the attempted hijacking of an Israel-bound FlyDubai plane.
When asked by reporters if he had been briefed about any links between Iran and the co-pilot who attacked his fellow pilot and attempted to crash the plane before being subdued by passengers, Mr. Trump said "we're working on it right now."
"I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes," Mr. Trump said. "But we're working on it right now."
Mr. Trump did not provide further details.
When asked if the co-pilot could have been placed by the IRGC, Mr. Trump said he "could've been, yeah."
In response to a question about potential U.S. retaliation if Tehran was connected to the attack, Mr. Trump said "they'll be hit, very hard, don't worry."
U.N. "deeply concerned" about impact of war on Lebanon's food supplies
The deputy director-general of the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization said Thursday that she was "deeply concerned" about the impact of the latest Israel-Hezbollah conflict on agriculture in south Lebanon.
Beth Bechdol said reports estimate that about 22% of Lebanon's agricultural land has been damaged or otherwise affected.
The damage "puts additional pressure on farmers and rural communities that, frankly, were already facing considerable hardships," said the FAO's Beth Bechdol. Bechdol added that she is "very concerned about just general food security levels" in Lebanon.
Hundreds of thousands remain displaced in Lebanon. While violence has decreased since a June ceasefire, Israeli troops remain in a "security zone" within the country and have been carrying out widespread demolitions affecting villages and farmland. Bechdol also expressed concern about potential contamination and soil damage in south Lebanon due to unexploded ordnance and residues from military operations.
In June, a U.N.-backed assessment from Lebanese authorities estimated agricultural production losses in south Lebanon this year had reached at least $530 million. The conflict has also "disrupted markets and reduced access" to essentials for food production, including fertilizer, Bechdol said.
This week, UNICEF said four in five households in Lebanon "are struggling to afford basic necessities as conflict compounds years of economic crisis." In April, a UN-backed report said more than 1.2 million people in Lebanon were expected to face acute hunger in the following months due to the latest war.
Iranian-U.K. dual national arrested on terror charges in connection with RAF Fairford incident
British counterterrorism police have arrested an Iranian-United Kingdom dual national in London in connection with the investigation into a security in England. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham previously said there were "strong indications" in the suspicious activity.
The 27-year-old man, who has not been otherwise identified, was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist attacks, police said.
A second man, a 26-year-old U.K. national, has also been questioned, police said. Two properties have been searched.
"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," said senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing Vicki Evans. "As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement."
Five men were arrested near the base, which has been used by U.S. warplanes carrying out strikes on Iran, on Sunday. On Monday, they were released on bail without any criminal charges, a move that . They remain out on bail, counterterror police said.
The nature of the incident remains unclear, and police have said no viable explosives or weapons were discovered. Burnham said Wednesday that there were indications Iran was involved. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel warned Britain that Iran was planning an attack on an air base weeks before the incident.

articles.summary: Don't Let Flydubai Terror Scare Derail Abraham Accords Progress  townhall.com
articles.full_text:
Terrorists want nothing more than to prevent peace.
It's why they fly planes into buildings, don explosive vests, and rain indiscriminate missiles on civilian populations.
The response to such terrorism isn't to cower. It is to lead with boldness, courage, and, sometimes, outright heroism.
The world just saw precisely such heroism in the high drama aboard Flydubai Flight 1073, from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
There was the Indian national pilot, Smit Machchhar, who, though bleeding badly after he was brutally stabbed by his terrorist, Omani national copilot, had the presence of mind to open the cockpit door as the plane nosedived 10,000 feet a minute.
There were the ordinary Israeli citizens — and above all, new national hero Yaniv Hayoun — who, Todd Beamer-style, swiftly rushed the cockpit and subdued the terrorist in a chokehold (yes, really).
There were the two off-duty pilots — reportedly British, South African, or New Zealander in nationality — who were able to glide the plane to a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
There was the Emirati flight crew, which handled the madness with aplomb, preventing chaos in a terrified cabin and ensuring the safety of all passengers.
Israeli activist Hillel Fuld quoted a military pilot on X: "In virtually every historical incident where an airliner got anywhere close to these speeds, the tail ripped off the entire back of the plane."
In the Book of Esther in the Hebrew Bible, God is not mentioned once. This is deliberate. His name doesn't need to appear: His presence is felt and seen everywhere.
It was the same way aboard Flydubai Flight 1073.
Some have reacted to this mesmerizing story in knee-jerk fashion. They have leaped to call for the full cancellation of all direct flights between Israel and the United Arab Emirates — and perhaps a downgrading of ties between Israel and the Arab world, more generally.
The instinct is understandable. The anti-Israel press downplayed the harrowing affair as a "pilot altercation," but the fact is a Muslim pilot tried to crash a plane full of Jews. That looks like terrorism. That's certainly what the Israelis think happened.
But terror attacks and near-terror attacks must not derail peace. To allow peace to be derailed is actually to do the terrorists' bidding.
The Abraham Accords, those dynamic 2020 peace agreements that normalized Israeli relations with the UAE, Bahrain, and Morocco, must go on.
Indeed, they must expand.
Many predicted the Abraham Accords would die after the Hamas savagery of October 7, 2023, and the ensuing war in Gaza.

That's why, just days before the near catastrophe aboard Flydubai Flight 1073, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu flew to Abu Dhabi to meet with representatives from eight different Arab countries.
Prior to that confab, Netanyahu rendezvoused directly with Emirati President Mohamed bin Zayed. It was the first time such a bilateral meeting was publicly verified by both countries.
Perhaps, then, the attempted terror attack timing isn't a coincidence. The rumor mill has also been swirling that Kuwait might soon join the Abraham Accords.
It's not hard to see what is going on here.
Before the October 7 pogrom, Saudi Arabia — the de facto leader of the Arab world — was on the precipice of making peace with Israel. Netanyahu dedicated much of his September 2023 address to the United Nations General Assembly to the topic. Around the same time, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman told Fox News' Bret Baier: "Every day we get closer" to normalization with Israel.
Peace seemed imminent.
One of Hamas' aims with its massacre was to derail Israeli-Saudi normalization. In that, Hamas was successful — for now.
But in the long run, Hamas won't be successful. Despite the setback, the House of Saud still knows that peace with Israel is an inevitability.
We cannot allow this week's would-be terrorist copilot to be successful, either.
This is not the time to pump the diplomatic brakes.
We might have to brace ourselves for additional attempted terror attacks, as cynics once again try to stop peace. Israel is undoubtedly prepared for that. The Arab states should prepare too.
Israel should also reevaluate its aviation procedures. Perhaps Israeli authorities can help vet inbound and outbound commercial pilots.

articles.title: Iranian press sees diplomacy alive but narrowing after US response - Iran International
articles.summary: Iranian press sees diplomacy alive but narrowing after US response  Iran International
articles.full_text:
Tehran media see diplomacy with Washington as increasingly precarious but not yet dead, with the two sides far apart over the sequencing of any deal and the window for compromise appearing to narrow.
Iran has disputed US accounts that Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his delegation to leave the country after indirect negotiations in New York reached a stalemate.
Iran’s UN mission said the delegation left according to a schedule communicated to the State Department on September 17 and dismissed reports of a US-mandated departure as “baseless and worthless.”
Two US officials told the Associated Press that Rubio ordered the delegation to leave after little progress in indirect talks mediated by Qatar.
The dispute follows Washington’s response to Iran’s seven-point proposal for de-escalation and reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Araghchi has said Tehran has made no changes to the proposal, which calls for lifting the blockade and unfreezing Iranian assets as steps toward reopening maritime transit and resuming nuclear negotiations.
Iranian media have nevertheless stopped short of declaring the diplomatic process dead.
Across outlets ranging from the government’s Iran Newspaper and state broadcaster-affiliated Jam-e Jam to the moderate business daily Donya-ye Eghtesad, the negotiations are portrayed as a stalled bargaining process rather than a complete collapse.
Washington’s response, delivered through Qatar, is seen as keeping the diplomatic channel open even as the two sides remain far apart.
Across the three outlets, four broad conclusions emerge.
First, no comprehensive settlement appears close. Even the more optimistic assessments envisage, at best, a phased arrangement focused initially on crisis management rather than a broader breakthrough.
Second, trust remains a central constraint. Iran Newspaper and Jam-e Jam cite the US withdrawal from the JCPOA in 2018 and subsequent American policy, while Donya-ye Eghtesad frames the problem more neutrally as the enduring question of which side should move first.
Third, the central dispute is increasingly about sequencing. Tehran wants an end to hostilities, sanctions and blockade relief before reopening Hormuz within seven days and moving to nuclear talks. Washington wants nuclear concessions and movement on Hormuz before easing pressure.
Fourth, from Tehran’s perspective, the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding remains the principal reference point. The Iranian press portrays the seven-day plan as an accelerated version of the June framework rather than a departure from it.
As the government’s voice, Iran Newspaper presents the seven-point proposal as a reasonable sequence that Washington is obstructing.
It also turns its attention to actors it sees as working against diplomacy, linking Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to the UAE and his reported intelligence briefing there to efforts to build regional opposition to Iran.
Jam-e Jam similarly rejects accusations that Tehran is seeking to avoid the nuclear issue, arguing that the proposal would bring forward the start of nuclear negotiations from roughly 60 days to seven.
Donya-ye Eghtesad, however, focuses more heavily on the costs of prolonged deadlock. It treats the US response as a test of Iran’s willingness to show nuclear flexibility and argues that verifiable limits on its program would improve the prospects for an agreement.
Despite their different political orientations, the three outlets broadly treat the seven-point plan as the basis for further negotiations rather than something Tehran should abandon.
The remaining debate is largely about timing.
Iran Newspaper and Jam-e Jam argue that leverage over Hormuz, combined with US pre-election concerns about energy prices, favors Tehran holding firm. Donya-ye Eghtesad warns instead that the diplomatic window could close within weeks and that the risks of waiting until after the election may outweigh the benefits.
Trump’s rejection of key Iranian demands, Israeli intelligence activity and the UAE’s acknowledgement of Netanyahu’s visit also provide ammunition to voices in Tehran arguing against early concessions.
Jam-e Jam compared the diplomatic process to a game of Snakes and Ladders, in which every advance is followed by a setback. For now, it sees the US midterm elections as the next major variable that could alter the calculations of either side.
